docs.title: Home
docs.text:
By Chris Blattman, political economist at UChicago.

In January 2026 I started playing with Claude Code. I had no idea what I was doing, but a little advice, time, and experimentation changed how I work.

Now I use AI as an executive assistant, project manager, and research collaborator. It helps me stay on top of commitments, manage complicated projects, and work through ideas. It also plans family vacations and home repairs.

I appreciated the help from colleagues, and so I built this site to help others. Beginners can start with the essentials, advanced users with the next steps or added workflows.

docs.title: About Chris Blattman
docs.text:
I'm a political economist at the Harris School of Public Policy at the University of Chicago. My research focuses on violence, crime, and poverty. I design and test interventions in cities across Latin America and Africa.

  • I write about research, conflict, policy, and increasingly about AI tools on X/Twitter (@cblatts) and at chrisblattman.com.
  • I've written a book about the causes of war and peace: Why We Fight.
  • For over a decade I've written practical advice on my blog for students, PhD researchers, and faculty, including how to write well.

docs.title: The team behind this site
docs.text:
These guides grow out of the AI workflows I use for research, administration, and everyday life. Shay Houseknecht worked with me on the October 2026 site refresh, turning my personal workflows with AI into practical walkthroughs.

We build and revise this site with the same AI tools we teach you to use. My research assistants help test, maintain, and improve the workflows. I also ask research staff, collaborators, and other principal investigators how they're using AI, where they're getting stuck, and what practical guidance would help. Those conversations help shape what we cover here. The site draws on others who share their approaches publicly; you'll find those influences on the Resources page.

docs.title: About the project
docs.text:
“Claude Blattman” is my name for this evolving setup. I started building it in January 2026 to get more of the help I wanted from an executive assistant, a project manager, and a research collaborator. My AI principles explains how I use it and what I've learned.

We share the guides, skills, and templates freely so you can adapt them to your own work. The source is on GitHub, under the MIT License. The site is built with Material for MkDocs and hosted on GitHub Pages.

docs.title: AI Concerns
docs.text: There are legitimate reservations about using AI at work. I won't try to answer all of them here, or settle the larger debates about jobs and society. A few balanced places to read about those debates are at the end. These are practical questions about the workflows on this site: getting useful help, deciding what to delegate, and making the investment worthwhile. My answers come mostly from experience, including some bets that may turn out to be wrong.

docs.title: “I'm getting slop.”
docs.text:
A polished draft that misses the point is still a bad draft, whether it comes straight from AI or a colleague passes it along.

On structured, recurring work, I think very high quality is possible. I've had good results with emails and project reports, and in my work, proposals and applications for ethics approval. These documents still require original ideas and difficult decisions. Their familiar structure gives AI a useful starting point. For a distinctive piece of writing, such as an op-ed or a book chapter, I'm much less satisfied with it producing the final prose. It helps me investigate ideas and work out the argument, then I do much more of the writing myself.

Getting good work takes an investment. I use agents that can read project files and carry a job through several steps. I give them earlier examples, explain what they got wrong, and work with them to improve the result.

Take a proposal. An earlier one shows AI the kind of document we need. It cannot tell the agent what we want to do this time, why we think it will work, or which difficult choices we have made. I set it up to ask me or a colleague for that missing information before drafting. Answering those questions is part of developing the proposal. It gets the thinking into the conversation before smooth prose can cover up what nobody has decided.

For a substantial task, I ask agents to develop approaches independently. I react to what comes back, explain what they misunderstood, and have fresh reviewers challenge the revised plan or draft. I want them to question my reactions too. Independent attempts and fresh criticism, alongside my own judgment, have made a large difference to the work I get. The result is a first draft I can refine instead of starting over.

My edits can also help the next task. I ask AI to compare my version with its draft and save useful lessons in the instructions or examples it will consult again. Correcting one conversation doesn't automatically improve the next one. Saving the lesson changes what it has to work with. It doesn't retrain the underlying model.

You can try a small version in a chatbot: give it a good earlier example and your rough points, then ask what it needs to know before drafting. Expect a conversation about what comes back.

What about invented facts, citations and confident mistakes?

Mistakes still happen. I don't personally fact-check everything AI produces. For important work, I keep people involved. For less consequential work, I'm happy to accept some errors in return for getting much more done. I don't need every task to be error-free for the help to be valuable.

I hear this concern less than I did a year or two ago. My impression is that the systems have improved, and people are learning to use them better. On the kinds of tasks my agents do well, I also feel I see fewer factual and citation errors than in first drafts I used to delegate to people. That's an impression, not a measured comparison.

Several agents can repeat the same mistake. Their agreement doesn't make a claim true. I can often tell when a proposal misses my point or a draft sounds nothing like me. Work I can't judge is harder, and adding reviewers doesn't make that difficulty disappear.

Will polished work make quality harder to distinguish?

This hasn't been a major problem for me so far. I also see room for AI to level the playing field by helping people consider things they would otherwise miss and learn from the process. Used poorly, it can encourage sloppy thinking.

My guess is that polished applications and pitches will tell us less about who can do the job. We'll turn to other forms of assessment and put more weight on reputation and demonstrated ability to carry something through. That could make it harder for newcomers without a track record to distinguish themselves through writing alone, even when AI has helped them produce better work.

docs.title: “Will I lose my voice, originality or credibility?”
docs.text:
For routine documents, I don't think good AI-assisted work has to cost me any of those things. An email that expresses my thoughts in language I'm happy with can be good enough for its audience. I don't need to write every first draft myself.

I dictate my points and give AI examples of my writing. I ask it to use my ideas without adding its own. When I want new ideas, I ask for them separately and decide what to use. Teaching it my voice produces a first draft that sounds enough like me to save a great deal of time. It still needs my judgment and edits.

For academic papers and most public articles, I want to do much more of the writing myself. My professional reputation rests on the argument and the wording. AI can help with research and criticism, but a draft I'd accept for an internal memo can take a lot of work before I want it to represent me in public.

The purpose and the rules matter. A school assignment meant to assess your own writing has a different standard from a routine report. This page and my principles essay are examples where I've chosen more AI assistance and disclosed it. The tool's ability to write a draft doesn't settle how much I want to delegate.

docs.title: “Can I give it confidential work?”
docs.text:
I'm not a security expert, and advice in this area is changing quickly. For proprietary business material, client information or colleagues' correspondence, I'd start with your organization's approved AI service. If your company doesn't have one, or you run a small business, look for a suitable business or enterprise arrangement and exercise caution.

Check which account you're using, how it's configured, and what information you're allowed to give it. Approval comes with conditions. A business label alone doesn't settle those questions. A promise not to train on your information also doesn't mean the provider won't store it.

If you bring another AI into the work, its account needs approval for the same material. A personal subscription doesn't override your organization's rules or requirements from a client, funder or journal. If work restricts agents, there are still ways to learn with approved tools and personal projects.

If you make these decisions for an organization, I think there are big advantages to giving people capable approved tools and as much practical freedom within them as possible. My worry is that restrictions which make the tools unhelpful encourage people to use unmanaged personal accounts. I'd much rather let them do ambitious work inside an arrangement the organization can manage.

Personally, I'm relatively risk-accepting. Connecting my email and project material lets the assistant find what it needs. I spend less time gathering and explaining it. For me, the benefits outweigh the disadvantages and risks, under considerable uncertainty. You can choose differently. My willingness to accept risk doesn't remove confidentiality obligations. I've described my access choices in more detail.

docs.title: “Is the setup worth it if it will soon be obsolete?”
docs.text:
I don't know how much of mine will last. My bet is that the help more than repays the investment in the short term. Working closely with these tools is also teaching me how they work and where they fail. I think that understanding will give me an edge with whatever comes next, even if some of today's setup becomes unnecessary.

The cost is real. Some recurring tasks took weeks to get working well. At first, explaining and correcting the job could take as long as doing it myself. I invested that time because I knew I'd need the help again.

Start with one real job you need to do. Build on it if it helps. Reproducing my whole setup would be a terrible first assignment. When an old instruction or process gets in the way, I ask AI to help work out whether to change it or get rid of it.

docs.title: “Will this help me focus, or give me more things to monitor?”
docs.text:
It cuts both ways. AI helps me get started. A revision can feel enormous, and opening the project to ask for a few concrete next steps is much easier than facing the whole thing at once. Even a bad first draft gives me something to react to. Arguing about what's wrong gets me moving.

Being able to advance several projects at once brings real productivity too. I can get work underway that I would otherwise keep putting off. Handing over some preparation also helps me put the task down for a while. But getting five projects moving is a very effective way to avoid spending two uninterrupted hours writing.

AI can keep me with that writing by quickly finding information I need or helping me work through an idea. It can also tempt me toward the easier progress available somewhere else. Getting help still leaves me to decide which project deserves my afternoon.

Where can I read about the bigger questions?

This page leaves larger questions about jobs, inequality, the environment and human learning mostly aside. These are useful places to read further. They offer different kinds of evidence and arguments, not a consensus.

  • Jobs and inequality: David Autor's interview (January 2026) explains the opportunities and risks for workers. Compare Yale's labor-market tracker (October 2026) with Stanford's early employment indicators (October 2026). They examine different data and groups, and the patterns do not settle what AI caused.
  • Energy and environment: Hannah Ritchie at Our World in Data (July 2026) separates AI from other data-center demand and puts individual queries in context. Long agent runs use more than a simple chat question, and global averages can hide local strain.
  • Learning: These explainers describe a study of AI use in math practice and teacher-guided tutoring in Nigeria. The settings differ. Neither establishes that AI always helps or harms learning.
  • Power and governance: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor's AI as Normal Technology (April 2025) emphasizes institutions and how technology gets adopted. It is a deliberately skeptical perspective on rapid-takeoff predictions.

docs.title: What's New — April 2026
docs.text:
A month of workflow improvements, batched into two launches. Launch 1 went live April 17 with the seven pages below. Launch 2 partially shipped April 26 — the tips pipeline, the multi-critic council, and the rest of the daily-workflow skill versions are now public; the voice pack and the full prompt-architecture page are still pending.

TL;DR

Three threads run through this update:

  1. Session discipline — how to run long work across /rewind, /compact, /clear, /done, and plan mode without losing context.
  2. Sub-project routing — multi-task projects that don't collapse under their own sprawl.
  3. The boring daily workflow that earns its keep — meeting loop, weekly review, /recall for searching past sessions, and why I stripped ceremonial emphasis from my skills.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
A normal workflow day on this stack:

  1. Morning — /morning-brief runs before I sit down. I open the inbox; triage labels are already applied.
  2. First call — /pre-meeting-brief pulls context from WhatsApp, Gmail, Granola, and Google Docs. I read it on the way.
  3. During the call — Granola records. Claude Code stays idle.
  4. After the call — /post-meeting drafts the follow-up email with decisions and action items extracted from the transcript.
  5. Between calls — deep in a paper or proposal. When the session fills up, /rewind for wrong paths, /compact <hint> for stale exploration, /done when it's time to hand off to another machine.
  6. Stuck on something I've solved before? — /recall searches every past Claude Code and Codex transcript. Usually finds the answer in the second or third result.
  7. Week end — /weekly-review synthesizes project updates across transcripts, emails, and Google Docs. Takes an hour, covers a week.

Each piece has its own page below.

docs.title: Session management
docs.text: How to run long sessions without losing your place. Decision matrix for /rewind vs /compact <hint> vs /clear vs starting fresh. Covers the four /rewind restore modes, when compaction hints actually steer the summary, and the real hook names (there's no PostCompact hook — compaction-aware reinjection ties to SessionStart). This older session-management guide has been retired. See the current handoff guidance.

docs.title: Sub-project routing
docs.text: When a project has three or four parallel workstreams — say, a paper, a grant revision, a trip itinerary, and an RA pipeline — I don't want their context bleeding into each other. /start-task plus .claude/active-subproject.json handle the routing. Handoffs land in the right folder, and SessionStart knows which sub-task is active. Current guide to organizing projects →

docs.title: Meeting workflow end-to-end
docs.text: A four-step loop that replaces about 20 minutes of manual work per meeting. /pre-meeting-brief pulls context before. Granola records during. /post-meeting extracts decisions and action items after and drafts the follow-up email. Read more →

docs.title: Weekly review
docs.text: The 3-marker system (done / in-progress / blocked) with batch updates and Granola transcript handling. Synthesizes a week of multi-project work in about an hour. Output is a single document I can hand to an RA, a collaborator, or future-me. Read more →

docs.title: /recall — search every past session
docs.text: SQLite FTS5 full-text search with BM25 ranking over local Claude Code and Codex JSONL transcripts. Same-machine only. Installed it because I kept solving the same problem twice. Skill by arjunkmrm (MIT). Read more →

docs.title: Dial-back discipline
docs.text: Why I stripped CRITICAL, YOU MUST, and ABSOLUTELY from most of my skills. Ceremonial emphasis overtriggers Claude 4.5+ in tool-use paths and degrades output quality. The fix is positive examples instead of negative rules, and saving emphatic language for genuinely blocking security or data concerns. Read more →

docs.title: Prompt architecture (partial — expanded)
docs.text: Three new sections on the Prompt Engineering page: long-content ordering (put the document at the top, question at the bottom), system-vs-user prompt separation, and reusable constraint blocks (anti-hallucination, anti-bloat, scope guard, structured uncertainty, voice preservation). The full package — including a prompt-preferences template download — ships in Launch 2.

docs.title: April 26 — early Launch 2
docs.text: Eight skill files updated or shipped, plus one new agent. Three threads:

docs.title: Daily-workflow versions caught up
docs.text:
The skills the meeting workflow page already references, brought to current versions on a single push.

  • /post-meeting v1.0 → v1.7 — hollow-transcript guard, explicit sender choice (you vs. an AI EA identity), and a recipient rule that defaults to the full team minus low-frequency categories. Production-validated end-to-end on a real research-team meeting. Skill file →
  • /weekly-review v1.4 → v1.9.1 — strict YAML config parsing (loud failure on malformed .claude/CLAUDE.md), bundled helper scripts for multi-tab Google Doc writes, RTF/PDF transcript normalization, per-meeting hollow-transcript handling, document-comment processing. Two council reviews shaped the v1.9 series. Skill file →
  • /tips-curate v1.3 → v1.5 — end-of-run backlog check that prompts /tips-integrate when unprocessed HIGH-quality tips exceed 15. Replaces a standing biweekly calendar ritual. Skill file →

docs.title: /done v2.1 — sub-project routing rewritten
docs.text:
The session-capture skill grew the most this month. The v2.x series rewrote routing to put the current working directory ahead of stale state:

  • Rule 1, CWD precedence: if you're in a sub-folder with its own HANDOFF.md, route there regardless of any state file. The actual workspace beats whatever was set days ago.
  • Rule 2, fresh active state with a divergence guard: route to active-subproject.json only if the state was modified in the last 24 hours (or marked permanent) AND the session topic actually overlaps with the state's task name. The token-intersection check prevents silent misroutes when state is stale or pointing somewhere irrelevant.
  • Non-destructive fallback: when neither rule fires, /done writes session content to a project-root SESSION_LOG.md instead of overwriting any project-root HANDOFF.md you maintain by hand. That destructive path is removed, not guarded.

Skill file →

docs.title: /council and the tips pipeline are public
docs.text:
The two pieces I'd flagged as pending in the original Launch 2 list shipped together because they share a dispatch pattern.

  • /council v1.2 (NEW publicly) — parallel critic agents + a separate synthesis pass. Hard cap of 5 critics, single-round only, never majority-votes on narrative output. The --chef-skill mode works out of the box (no persona files required) for skill/tool-design reviews. Default panels (plan / paper / decision / grant) require persona agent files in ~/.claude/agents/. Skill file →
  • /tips-integrate v1.2 → v2.1 — Phase 1.5 dispatches a 5-persona council (Catalog Conflict / Maintenance Tax / Compounder / First-Run / Skeptic) before generating proposals. Composite scoring is mean(5 personas) − 0.1 × blocker_count — additive penalty, no clamping, the council ranks but doesn't dismiss. Top 3 auto-apply, items 4–7 one-tap, items 8–15 visible with full detail. Falls back to single-critic mode when the agent file is missing. Skill file →
  • agents/proposal-critic-agent.md (NEW publicly) — one parameterized agent file invoked five times in parallel, each with a different persona passed in the prompt. Bundled alongside /tips-integrate. Agent file →

docs.title: Continuous-improvement page consolidated
docs.text: The four-skill pipeline now has a single canonical page that explains how the parts fit together. Lede leads with the firehose problem (tips arrive faster than anyone can adopt them) and six concrete questions: which to adopt, where to store them, how to remember them, how to prioritize, how to get them into your workflow, how to avoid wrecking a working setup with a bad addition. The four stages (discover / curate / integrate / applied), a worked tip-to-rule-change example, the five critic personas, the actual changes the council has approved, install instructions, the tips log and learning-catalog mechanics — all in one place. Read the page →

A couple of pieces still waiting.

  • Voice pack system — register overlays (core voice + proposal + public writing + email) plus a critic-agent that flags drift at the line level. Shown as a complete pack with sanitized downloads. Gated on voice-pack sanitization.
  • Prompt architecture (full page) — the Prompt Engineering page got three new sections in the April 17 launch (long-content ordering, system-vs-user, constraint blocks). The complete page update plus the prompt-preferences template as a paste-into-any-project download is still pending.

docs.title: Stay updated
docs.text:
• Email updates — low volume, easy opt-out.
  • GitHub — star if useful; the repo is public.
  • Feedback — what's missing, what's wrong, what's confusing.

docs.title: Should I use Codex or Claude?
docs.text:
Start with either. If you already use one, keep it. If you already pay for Claude or ChatGPT, check what your plan includes before buying something else. The first-session guide walks you through choosing and opening your app, and explains why I currently prefer Codex.

I find Claude and Codex both good generalists. Their interfaces and connections differ, so start with the one that fits how you work. You can add another later.

docs.title: Do I need both Codex and Claude?
docs.text:
One is enough to start, including for a council of independent subagents. For important work, I recommend trying a second AI: I find the extra perspective worth paying for.

Start with an inexpensive subscription for a month and use it on work that matters to you. Then decide whether to upgrade or add a third. Using different AI models explains how to connect them and make them your default council.

docs.title: Should I pay for Grok and Gemini?
docs.text:
I use them for different reasons. Gemini often gives me different results and perspectives from Claude and Codex, so I include it in my default council. I use Grok for narrow questions about AI integrations and best practices, drawing on X/Twitter posts. It is not a regular member of my council.

You do not need my whole setup to get started. The model comparison explains what I get from each.

docs.title: What are agents?
docs.text:
An agent can work with your files and tools and carry out several steps toward a result. You give it a task, supply context, and correct its work as you go. A subagent is a separate worker your main agent starts and manages for you.

Try a real task in the first-session guide. The council walkthrough shows how to get several independent attempts and a review of the result.

docs.title: What are plugins?
docs.text:
A plugin bundles skills and their supporting files so you can install them together. A skill is a saved set of instructions for your agent.

The starter kit is one such bundle. /council develops the work with independent members and brings their findings together. /adversarial-review examines the draft with fresh reviewers. /done saves a handoff for your next session.

Ask your AI to help install the kit and explain what it adds. Plugins also give you a way to receive updates; ask the agent to check your installed version and how updates work in your app.

docs.title: What is a symlink?
docs.text:
A symlink is a pointer to a file or folder somewhere else. Opening the pointer takes you to the original. Editing through either path changes the same file.

This can help when an app expects an instructions file in a particular place, but you want to keep the actual file in a synced folder. You set up a pointer on each computer so the app can find that shared file.

Ask your agent to handle the setup:

Help me keep my standing instructions in my synced folder and connect them where this app expects to find them. Check that the connection works.

docs.title: What are Git and GitHub?
docs.text:
Git records saved versions of a project's files. Each saved checkpoint is called a commit. GitHub hosts these projects, called repositories, so people can share and work on them together. Repositories can be public or private.

My skills and templates live in a public GitHub repository. You can give your agent a link and ask it to read the instructions and help you use the files. The project organization guide shows how to put those files to work.

Git is also useful for keeping a history of your own work. Ask your agent to set it up and save checkpoints at useful milestones. You can return to those saved versions; Git does not automatically preserve every unsaved change.

docs.title: What is prompt engineering?
docs.text:
It means shaping a request to help an AI produce a useful result. For the work on this site, start by explaining what you want in ordinary language, as you would to a colleague. You can dictate several paragraphs; you do not need a polished prompt.

Give the agent the result you want, who it is for, the relevant material, constraints, and what good looks like. Examples and corrections help too. If you do not know the best approach, ask it to suggest one and ask you the questions that would change it.

The council walkthrough shows how to do this. Preferences you want applied repeatedly belong in standing instructions or your voice guides, so you do not have to explain them from scratch each time.

docs.title: Build a continuous improvement system
docs.text:
When I rewrite an AI’s draft, I want the next draft to benefit. At the end of the task, I can say: “Analyze my edits and send what you learned to the voice project.” The agent compares the versions and puts the useful observations where I can review and use them again.

That is what I mean by continuous improvement. My edits and complaints help improve the instructions, examples and organization I work with.

Start with the voice project you built on page one and a piece of writing you actually need. After editing a draft, ask the agent to compare your changes and identify what it should do differently next time. The agent handles the comparison and filing, and you decide which lessons should change your guidance.

As always, ask your AI to do the setup and walk you through it.

Open your AI app and navigate to the voice project folder you built on page one. Then ask:

Now that we've built our voice and style guidelines for writing, help me set up a system for continual updates as I edit agentic writing. Follow the walkthrough at claudeblattman.com.

docs.title: 1. Give your corrections a home
docs.text:
Use the voice project you already built. Keep the drafts with the work they belong to, and give the lessons a route back to that shared project. For example:

My voice/
├── CORE_VOICE.md          Preferences shared across writing types
├── EMAIL_VOICE.md         Email-specific guidance
├── LONG_FORM_VOICE.md     Long-form guidance, if needed
├── VOICE_LEARNING.md      How to compare edits and handle lessons
└── state/
    └── voice-learning/
        ├── CANDIDATE_INDEX.md       Index of corrections and decisions
        ├── CANDIDATE_TEMPLATE.md    Template for each correction record
        └── candidates/
            └── [correction-id].md   One record per correction episode

Funder presentation/
└── reviews/
    └── [revision]/
        ├── email-draft.md
        └── email-revised.md

This follows my storage structure. The writing project and draft filenames are examples; keep the original and revised versions with the work they belong to. Ask the agent to create the shared learning files and folders.

state/voice-learning/candidates/ — one record per correction episode, with changes, possible lessons, source links and the decision. CANDIDATE_INDEX.md — an index that helps the agent find those records. CANDIDATE_TEMPLATE.md — a consistent format for new records. VOICE_LEARNING.md — the procedure for comparing edits, filing observations and updating a guide when you agree to a change.

Saving a correction note does not, by itself, change the next draft. When you agree to a lasting preference, the agent updates the relevant voice guidance. Future writing sessions are instructed to read that guidance. The notes explain how you reached the decision; they are not another set of rules to load into every draft.

In my setup, writing and learning connect like this:

The voice improvement loop Ask the agent to draft something, revise the draft, and ask it to learn. The agent compares the saved versions and files a correction record with source links in your shared voice project. If you agree to a reusable lesson, it updates the core or relevant writing-type guide. The guides inform the next draft. If no new rule is needed, keep the notes and leave the guides unchanged. YOUR WRITING PROJECT YOUR SHARED VOICE PROJECT Ask the agent to draft something Uses CORE_VOICE.md EMAIL_VOICE.md Revise the draft; ask it to learn Saves, for example email-draft.md email-revised.md Agent compares your edits Follows VOICE_LEARNING.md File notes with source links; suggest a proposed lesson Files under voice-learning/ candidates/*.md CANDIDATE_INDEX.md Update the guide if you agree Updates the relevant guide CORE_VOICE.md EMAIL_VOICE.md No new rule? Keep notes. The voice guides inform your next draft

When I agree to a new preference, the agent updates CORE_VOICE.md or the relevant writing-type guide, such as EMAIL_VOICE.md. Saved instructions direct future sessions to those guides. Sometimes the comparison shows that the existing guidance already covers the correction; the agent records that outcome without adding another rule.

My voice project has a place for correction records and a learning procedure.

docs.title: 2. Make learning from edits a standing instruction
docs.text:
The standing instruction from page one already tells your agent to use your voice guides. Extend it once so it also knows how to save corrections from any writing project:

When I say “compare my edits,” “learn from my edits,” or “analyze my edits and send what you learned to the voice project,” follow the instructions in my voice learning Markdown file and update the necessary logs. Add this to my global CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md instructions, preserving my other instructions.

If you use both Claude and Codex, do this once in each app.

I've updated my global instructions so that my agents know where to save corrections.

docs.title: Make a correction useful next time
3. Correct a real piece of work
docs.text:
Use your voice pack on a real draft. Then edit it, or explain what is wrong. Read for meaning before judging resemblance: the reasoning, uncertainty, tone, amount of explanation and organization all matter.

For example:

They already know the background. Keep the reason for the delay, thank them for the work, then make the question easy to find.

That gives the agent more to work with than “This doesn't sound like me.”

I've given my own feedback to a draft AI wrote for me.

docs.title: 4. Ask the agent to store what it learned
docs.text:
Once the revision says what you mean, ask:

Analyze my edits and send what you learned to the voice project.

Let the agent find the versions and do the comparison. Even if you edited elsewhere, you can say “Analyze my edits” and the agent will look for the latest draft in the files or connected apps it can access. If it cannot find the original draft, it should say so.

You should get a short explanation and a link to the saved record. For example, the agent might reply:

You removed several technical follow-up requests while keeping the main findings and questions. Your email guide already says to keep an initial response focused on the next conversation; I didn't apply that well here. I've saved the comparison and linked it from your correction index. I haven't changed the guide.

That illustrative response reflects one of my recent email revisions. The comparison showed that the existing guidance covered the problem. When it finds a useful new preference instead, the agent should suggest a lesson and show how it would update the relevant guide.

For a project-specific revision you only want to log, say:

Save this revision and a short record of what changed. These changes are specific to this project, so I don't think we need to update my voice guide.

This saves the versions with the writing project and a project-only record in the shared correction index. You get a record without turning a one-off change into a writing rule.

I've saved the correction and received the agent's response.

docs.title: 5. Update the guidance if it’s useful for future drafts
docs.text:
If there is a change to make, have the agent put it in the smallest useful place. You can do this in the same conversation:

Yes, update the voice guidelines. Replace any rule it supersedes, keep a recoverable previous version, and record the decision and its scope in our notes.

I've made a personal judgment on whether or not to update the voice guide.

docs.title: Repair the way you work together
docs.text:
What if the next draft still misses the mark?

If it failed, ask the agent to distinguish three things: Did it read the guide? Did it apply the relevant preference? Did that preference help? A missing file needs a working connection. An ignored instruction needs better application and review. A preference that makes the writing worse needs narrowing or removal. Adding another rule is not always the answer.

docs.title: 6. Revisit the setup when real work gives you a reason
docs.text:
Sometimes AI gets fixated on an instruction from three months ago, or starts doing badly at a task it handled well before. Use a council to diagnose it! Describe the failure and ask:

Use a council to diagnose why this task used to work better. Read the relevant instructions, examples and recent corrections. Check for stale or conflicting guidance, missing context, and instructions that were not loaded. Propose the smallest useful repair, explain what it would replace, and let me review it before making the change.

The repair may be to clarify an instruction, change where information is stored, or delete a rule.

Let real work tell you when to revisit the setup. Start with consequential corrections and check what happens next. As the tools improve, some of the organization you once needed may become less useful.

I know how to diagnose a recurring problem and revise the system when needed.

docs.title: A caveat
docs.text: I used a council to help me set up this recurring improvement system. We considered both the approach above and building it into a formal skill. You might prefer a skill for invoking the same note-taking and improvement procedure; it can use the same files and workflow.

docs.title: My AI principles
docs.text:
How I use AI to stay on top of work and life

AI has become the team I always wanted: an executive assistant, a project manager, and a research collaborator. The job changes with the problem. It helps me keep a research team moving, investigate an idea, or decide what to do about a broken water heater. Family vacations count too.

I had plenty of work for this team. Thousands of unread emails were serving as my to-do list. So were items in my calendar. I was behind on referee reports and recommendation letters, and going into meetings trying to reconstruct where we had left off. I needed to be on top of my projects to keep everyone else on top of them.

AI even helped me write this essay. I've been trying to teach it to write like me. I dictated the ideas and examples, gave it my previous writing as a guide, and went back and forth over what it got wrong. AI wrote the first draft. It doesn't get my voice quite right, but iterating with it is much faster for me than writing from scratch. I get more done, and the basic idea gets out there.

This is one example of what the help looks like. At the very least, I get a first draft I can rewrite or a first answer I can work on.

There is a startup cost. I have to explain the job, provide the background, and correct what comes back. Getting some recurring tasks to work well took weeks. At first, it could take as long as doing the work myself. I made that investment because I knew I would need the help again.

The biggest gains have come from using independent agents and improving the way we work together. I ask several agents to develop approaches or challenge a draft, add my own judgment, and use what went wrong to make the next attempt better.

I discuss practical reservations about working this way in AI Concerns, including quality, confidentiality and whether the setup is worth the trouble.

docs.title: Build up incrementally, one task or project at a time
docs.text:
Try one or two useful tasks in the first couple of days. Get used to explaining what you want, reacting to what comes back, and trying again. Then build from one task or project to the next. Reproducing my entire setup is a terrible first assignment.

The jobs that have mattered to me suggest several places to begin:

  • Get obligations out of your inbox. Working with AI, I shifted the commitments sitting in my unread email and calendar into Apple Reminders on my phone. This grew into an executive assistant project that helps me triage messages and reminders. A first attempt could be much smaller: take a few messages, identify what actually requires action, and put the confirmed tasks somewhere you will see them.

  • Get on top of one ongoing project. My research projects have large teams, complicated histories, and results or decisions that need my attention every week. AI helps me prepare to give useful directions. You might begin with the notes from the last meeting and two recent updates, then ask what needs deciding at the next meeting and what information is missing.

  • Make the next recurring document easier. A proposal or an application for ethics approval has to get done this week, but I know I will face a similar job again. I invest in the current document and in figuring out how to make the next one easier. Your starting point might be an old example, a new brief, and a draft you can edit.

  • Choose a problem from ordinary life. Family vacations, household purchases, expenses, and tax-planning questions have all been useful applications for me. A replacement water heater or an electronic family calendar can be a worthwhile one-time investigation. You don't need to turn every purchase into a permanent system.

Choose something you need to do and can judge. Once you get comfortable, give AI more of the job or try a project with more moving pieces.

docs.title: Ask AI to help work out the approach
docs.text:
Whenever I catch myself thinking “I don’t know how to do this with AI,” that is usually the next thing I ask it. I don’t know how to teach it my voice. I don’t know how to organize this project. I don’t know what information it needs to help with my email. Those are things we can work out together.

I describe what I want and what matters to me. I don't need to arrive with a polished prompt or know the best method, because figuring out the method is part of the job. For questions about tools and setup, I ask it to look into current practices.

For an unfamiliar project, I sometimes ask several independent agents to propose an approach and tell me what they need to know first. I answer their questions, react to the proposal, and have a fresh set of agents review it critically and constructively. This was especially useful when I was getting started. I still do it when I have little idea how to begin.

When something breaks, I describe the problem and ask AI to investigate. I don't need to know which instruction is wrong or where the repair belongs. What I need is a diagnosis I can understand and react to.

docs.title: Make independent agents part of the way you work
docs.text:
For a difficult question, I want more than one agent’s first answer. I want different approaches, different arguments, and someone looking for what the others missed.

Sometimes I ask separate instances of the same AI to tackle a question. Sometimes I use different AIs. They work independently, then another agent brings the results together. I call this a council, and I use councils for a great deal of my work. Asking one chat to play several characters doesn't give me the same independent attempts. I want to see useful disagreements, including the concern that only one reviewer raised.

I use these agents for different jobs. I can divide an investigation into separate questions, ask for competing ways to frame an argument, or have several reviewers examine the same plan. An alternative I reject can still help me figure out what I think.

Several agents can still repeat the same mistake. I ask them to examine disagreements and the reasons behind their answers, rather than treat a vote as the answer. I'm relying on them to do much of that investigation. I don't independently check everything they produce.

docs.title: Have a fresh council challenge the plan, then revise it
docs.text:
Once we have what looks like a good plan, I often ask a fresh council to find what's wrong with it. I give feedback too, and that cycle of planning, criticism, and revision accounts for a large part of the improvement I get from these tools.

The sequence looks something like this:

  1. Explain the job and have agents investigate or propose approaches independently.

  2. Bring their findings together, retaining the disagreements that matter.

  3. Add my judgment: what I actually want, which constraints they missed, and where the plan makes no sense to me.

  4. Have fresh reviewers examine the revised plan, with the relevant evidence and constraints.

  5. Revise the plan and use it for the job. Give feedback on what comes back, and return to the review when there is a problem worth another pass.

The fresh reviewers need the job, the evidence, and the constraints. They don't need the entire conversation that persuaded the first group. I want something I can act on: a bad assumption, a missing dependency, an alternative worth trying. They should also be free to say the plan looks sound.

I can often tell when a proposal misses the argument I want to make, a recommendation misunderstands my priorities, or a draft sounds nothing like me. I edit it or explain the problem. Work I can't judge is harder. Several reviewers help, but they don't make that difficulty disappear.

In my experience, this cycle makes an enormous difference to whether I can actually use the result (though I haven't measured the benefit of each additional review).

Another pass needs a job. Sometimes it's worth checking an important point again. Sometimes the agents are just rearranging the adjectives and it is time to get on with the work. Agreement doesn't make an answer true, and not every objection deserves a repair.

docs.title: Teach it with examples and corrections
docs.text:
A review improves the task in front of me. Examples and corrections can make the next one easier. A recommendation letter is a perfect snowflake, but it still has a structure and a voice. My old letters give AI something concrete to learn from. They can't decide where I place a new student relative to others I have recommended, or what I think is strongest about the student’s work. I have to supply those judgments.

Referee reports show how the process develops. I read the paper and dictate my comments. AI can help me examine a claim I am uncertain about, then turn my comments into a draft using my previous reports as examples. I edit that draft myself and say how I used AI. The confidentiality rules that apply to a report still govern what I can give a tool.

Finishing the report is also a chance to improve the next one. Correcting the current conversation doesn't necessarily change the next one. So I ask AI to compare my edited version with its draft and work out what it should do differently. Then I ask it to save useful lessons in the instructions or examples it will use again.

I also ask where the lesson belongs. A correction to a project’s budget should stay with that project. A recurring problem with my voice might belong in the writing instructions. AI can help decide what to save and where. Otherwise, I'll be explaining the same mistake next time.

docs.title: Keep improving the system, including removing what no longer helps
docs.text:
Over weeks and months, I also use corrections to change how the whole project works. Call it recursive improvement: using AI to help improve the way I use AI.

My corrections change the instructions, examples, or organization it will use next time. Editing a paragraph doesn't retrain the underlying model.

Every so often, AI gets fixated on something I told it three months ago. Or it starts doing badly at a job it used to handle well. I ask it to diagnose the problem, sometimes with several independent opinions. We might clarify an instruction, move some information, or delete a rule. For a large setup, I take a broader look every few months.

Even the organization can become unnecessary. I used to put more effort into rolling summaries of research projects. As the tools improved, some of those summaries seemed less essential. More files and more instructions aren't automatically an improvement. When an old instruction or process is getting in the way, I ask AI to help me work out what has become unnecessary.

docs.title: Organization pays off, especially when you work in projects
docs.text:
Each research project has a home, with its papers, correspondence and decisions. So do the committees I sit on, home repairs and family vacations. When I open a project, I want to pick up where we left off.

My projects in Codex largely reflect how I've organized my hard drive. I already had a reasonably organized collection of folders in Dropbox. One of the jobs I gave AI in the first months was helping me reorganize that Dropbox. It wasn't my first task.

I ask AI to help organize what it needs to know: what we are trying to do, who is involved, what we have decided, and what still needs attention. It needs to distinguish an old proposal from a current decision. Saving those decisions and the next actions makes it easier to return.

Being organized doesn't mean putting every old document into every conversation. Keep the important current context easy to find, with a way to reach the background when needed. A long collection of unrelated instructions can make the job harder.

A lot of my work now happens in desktop tools with access to those folders, though keeping related work together in a chatbot project is useful too. You can begin by supplying the notes and documents for one meeting, then ask what else is missing. You don't need to reorganize your whole drive first.

For a team meeting, I want to know what we were supposed to accomplish, what the new results mean, and what needs my attention. Preparation can turn into an investigation of a research question. Before exploring a new subject or deciding whether to write about it, I might want a researched briefing of two pages, five, or twenty. Having the project’s history available helps me ask better questions without reconstructing everything each time.

docs.title: Choose how much access to give it
docs.text:
I'm relatively risk-accepting about this. I have connected more of my email, calendar, WhatsApp, and meeting transcripts than many people would be comfortable with. There is a large benefit to an assistant that can gather the relevant material itself. I spend less time finding, copying, and explaining it.

For me, the benefits outweigh the costs and risks. Part of my trust comes from the companies’ financial stake in protecting users. A serious security failure would be costly for them. That gives them a reason to invest in protection, without telling me whether a particular connection or permission is safe.

I try to make deliberate choices about what the tools can reach. Much of my private information has lived in Dropbox for years. I use Selective Sync to keep especially sensitive Dropbox folders off my computer. Research data stays in university Box, with selective access rather than general access. I also ask AI to help with periodic security audits: what can it reach, what is unnecessarily exposed, and what should change? An AI-assisted audit can help identify problems, but it can't certify that nothing has been missed.

I also need to be clear about what those precautions accomplish. Dropbox’s online-only setting can download a file when it's opened. Selective Sync removes selected folders from the local drive, but a connected cloud account can provide another access route. Dropbox explains the difference and the separate access granted to connected apps. Storage location, permissions, and connected services are separate questions. Working from files on my hard drive doesn't mean the model processes them only on my computer. For example, Claude Code sends data to its model service. Limits on model training, data retention, and access are different protections.

Permission to read information is also different from permission to send, change, or delete it. For ordinary email, I want to approve the actual message before it's sent. A rule in a project file is an instruction, not a technical limit that prevents an action. The risk is also broader than a company getting hacked. An instruction hidden in a web page or email can try to redirect an agent that reads it. The possibility matters more when the same assistant can read private material and communicate outside the project. Anthropic describes this problem and the limits of its defenses.

There are also people whose risk I don't get to decide: research participants, colleagues, students, and anyone whose private information appears in a message or transcript. My willingness to take a risk doesn't settle their rights or the rules governing their data.

You will have to make your own choices about access. Begin with a few documents if that's what you're comfortable with. Expand when the benefit warrants it. My willingness to connect more of my life is a personal judgment.

docs.title: Decide which parts of the work to delegate
docs.text:
I also delegate different amounts of writing, depending on the job. AI can help draft routine emails and responses through several iterations, and I generally edit them myself. I spend less time polishing a casual reply. Proposals and applications for ethics approval can also start with a substantial AI draft, using my examples and refined by me.

For academic papers and most articles for a public audience, I generally want to do the writing myself. My professional reputation rests on this work, and I care about the argument and the wording. I also think a high AI share can undermine its credibility. This essay is an exception: I've asked AI to do more of the writing and explained that at the start.

There is still a great deal of help to ask for while I write. AI can locate a source, interrogate an idea, identify an objection, or help me think through a theoretical problem. It can research an unfamiliar subject so I can decide what I think about it. Delegating the investigation and criticism can leave more of my attention for the writing I want to do myself.

Those boundaries depend on the piece and what I want from it. The tool’s ability to write a draft doesn't settle how much I want to delegate.

docs.title: Use the help to get moving—and to put things down
docs.text:
One benefit is how much easier it is to begin. A coauthor sends back a paper, and revising it feels enormous. I can open the project, ask AI to read what has come back, and help me find a few concrete things to do first. As with this essay, even a bad first pass gives me something to react to. Arguing about what is wrong gets me moving.

The help is also available at odd moments. With my computer on and my project material accessible, I can be at the gym at eight, remember a meeting at nine-thirty, and dictate what I need prepared from my phone. It works on the briefing while I finish my workout. I can scan it before the meeting, or during it to check what we have missed. You do not have to work from the gym. For me, being able to hand over the preparation helps me put it down for a while.

The overwhelming personal achievement has been becoming less of a hot mess. I feel more on top of things. That has helped the people I work with too. If anything, I have more staff than before, and they use these tools as well.

There is a catch. Getting five projects moving is a very effective way to avoid spending two uninterrupted hours writing. AI can keep me with an argument by finding the information I need, or tempt me away to something easier.

Getting help with five projects still leaves me to decide which one deserves my afternoon.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
Last updated: February 2026

This site respects your privacy. Here's what we collect and why.

docs.title: Analytics
docs.text:
This site uses GoatCounter, an open-source, privacy-friendly analytics tool. GoatCounter does not use cookies, does not track you across sites, and does not collect personal information. It counts page views so we know which guides are useful and which need work.

GoatCounter is free for non-commercial use and its code is fully open source. No data is shared with third parties. You can read their privacy policy for details.

docs.title: Email Updates
docs.text:
If you sign up for email updates, we store your email address through Buttondown, a newsletter service based in the United States. We use it to send occasional updates when new tools or guides are added — typically a few times per year.

We do not share, sell, or use your email for any other purpose.

docs.title: Your Rights
docs.text:
• Unsubscribe from any email using the link at the bottom of every message.
  • Request deletion of your email by writing to claudeblattman+privacy@gmail.com.

docs.title: Tools and Workflows
docs.text:
This site teaches workflows using Claude Code, MCP integrations, and other AI tools. This privacy page covers the website only — not the tools themselves.

For data handling when using Claude Code and MCP integrations, see:

  • Privacy & Setup (Tax Workflow) — the most detailed treatment, covering data flow, API transmission, and what stays local
  • Anthropic's privacy policy — how Anthropic handles API data
  • MCP Setup — scope of each integration

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: If you have questions about how your data is handled, contact claudeblattman+privacy@gmail.com.

docs.title: Resources and Influences
docs.text:
A curated collection of the resources, tools, and reference implementations that shaped this project. Each entry includes a brief summary of what's useful and why I found it worth your time.

Thanks to Anup Malani for being my first tutor on the basics — he's the one who got me started with Claude Code and showed me what was possible.

docs.title: Reference Implementations
docs.text: These are the projects and posts that most influenced how I built my system. If you want to see how other people are doing this, start here.

docs.title: Aniket Panjwani — AI Economist
docs.text:
Aniket's advice has been an important influence on how I use AI. His guide to agentic coding covers working with agents, organizing project context and improving recurring workflows. Its examples focus on economists, but many of the habits apply more broadly.

Aniket Me is a skill I developed to apply his public advice to the work you give your agent. It includes links to the original sources and works with Claude Code and Codex. It is an independent adaptation, not Aniket himself or an endorsement by him.

docs.title: Boris Tane — How I Use Claude Code
docs.text:
boristane.com

A developer's opinionated workflow with Claude Code. The Research → Plan → Annotate → Implement structure he describes became the backbone of how I think about multi-step tasks. His use of persistent markdown files as shared state between Claude and the user directly influenced my CLAUDE.md approach. Well-written and confident — one of the first posts that made me think this was more than a toy.

docs.title: Pedro Sant'Anna — Claude Code My Workflow
docs.text:
psantanna.com

The closest thing to what I'm building, but for econometrics. Pedro is an academic (economics) who built an ambitious system with 10 agents and 19 commands. His MEMORY.md pattern for persistent learning across sessions was an early influence. His research-specific slash commands showed me what was possible. Fair warning: the complexity can be overwhelming for beginners — I deliberately kept my system simpler.

docs.title: Mike Murchison — Claude Chief of Staff
docs.text:
GitHub

A four-pillar structure (Communicate, Learn, Deepen Relationships, Achieve Goals) for using Claude as an executive assistant. The Goals.yaml as a single source of truth, the /gm morning briefing command, and the idea of CLAUDE.md as "your AI operating system" all shaped my approach. My /morning-brief and /checkin skills descend directly from this repo.

docs.title: Dave Killeen — Dex
docs.text:
GitHub

An extension of Murchison's Chief of Staff pattern that adds structured pillars (pillars.yaml), session learnings capture, and usage logging. If Murchison's repo is the architecture, Dex is the operational layer. I used it alongside the original when designing my session capture (/done) and goal alignment (/goals-review) skills. Discovered February 2026.

docs.title: Obie Fernandez — Building a Personal CTO Operating System
docs.text:
Medium

A real workflow where Claude Code acts as an EA for a CTO: managing priorities, shipping work, and maintaining an operational cadence. What's useful here isn't the CTO-specific parts — it's the pattern of encoding your daily rhythm into skills so Claude runs your system instead of you running Claude. The "operating system" framing influenced how I think about the whole EA layer.

docs.title: Chris Wiles — Claude Code Showcase
docs.text:
GitHub

A full example of a .claude/ directory structure with hooks, skills, agents, commands, and GitHub workflows. If you want to see what a well-organized Claude Code project looks like before building your own, this is the best single reference. I used it as a structural template when organizing my own skills and hooks directories.

docs.title: Ethan Mollick — One Useful Thing
docs.text:
oneusefulthing.org

Ethan's blog is the gold standard for writing about AI for non-technical professionals. His Models / Apps / Harnesses framework helped me think about where different tools fit. Key insight that stuck with me: "the shift from chatbot to agent is the most important change since ChatGPT launched." If you read one person on AI and work, make it Ethan.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
docs.anthropic.com

The official setup, configuration, and usage guide. Start here if you're installing Claude Code for the first time. Covers CLAUDE.md, MCP integrations, slash commands, and the permission model. The docs have improved significantly — they're now genuinely useful as a reference.

docs.title: Claude Code Best Practices
docs.text:
code.claude.com

Anthropic's comprehensive best practices guide: context management, CLAUDE.md conventions, subagent patterns, parallel sessions, and common failure modes. If you read one official guide, make it this one.

docs.title: Anthropic Skills Repository
docs.text:
github.com/anthropics/skills

Anthropic's official collection of example Agent Skills — the first-party reference for skill structure, YAML frontmatter conventions, and the SKILL.md format. Useful as a template when building your own.

docs.title: Anthropic Prompt Engineering Guide
docs.text:
docs.anthropic.com

Anthropic's own guide to writing effective prompts. More technical than this site goes, but worth reading if you want to understand the mechanics. I adapted several patterns from here into my prompt formatting skills.

docs.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
docs.text:
modelcontextprotocol.io

The protocol that lets Claude Code talk to Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Docs, and other services. Understanding MCP is essential if you want to build integrations beyond what I've packaged. The spec is well-documented; the ecosystem is growing fast.

docs.title: MkDocs Material
docs.text:
squidfunk.github.io

The framework this site is built with. If you want to build something similar — a documentation site for your own tools or research — Material is the best option I've found. Free, well-maintained, and the configuration is all YAML (no JavaScript required).

docs.title: AI for Economists
docs.text: This site focuses on project management, communication, and workflow automation. But the biggest wave of AI adoption in economics is around data analysis, statistical coding, and empirical methods — areas I haven't covered yet (coming soon). These are the essential resources for that side of the work.

docs.title: Anton Korinek — Generative AI for Economic Research
docs.text:
JEL Paper (AEA) · AI Agents Update (NBER, 2025) · Substack

The authoritative academic treatment. Korinek's 2023 Journal of Economic Literature paper identifies six use case domains for LLMs in economics (ideation, writing, background research, data analysis, coding, mathematical derivations) and has been updated twice — most recently with an NBER working paper on AI agents for autonomous literature reviews, econometric coding, and data analysis. If you read one academic paper on this topic, make it this one.

docs.title: Scott Cunningham — MixtapeTools
docs.text:
GitHub · Substack

A GitHub repo of tools for coding, teaching, and presentations with AI assistance — includes a "Referee 2" audit protocol for verifying empirical code across R/Stata/Python, a PDF reading skill for parsing academic papers, and a CLAUDE.md template for Claude Code sessions. Cunningham (author of Causal Inference: The Mixtape) also writes regularly about AI and causal inference on Substack.

docs.title: Awesome Econ AI Stuff
docs.text:
meleantonio.github.io

14+ curated AI skills across 7 categories (Analysis, Data, Theory, Writing, Communication, Literature, Ideation) designed for Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Includes skills that automate DiD/IV/RD coding in Stata and LaTeX paper writing. The closest thing to a skill library specifically for empirical economists.

docs.title: More Resources
docs.text:
Resource Focus Jesse Lastunen — AI for Economists Worked prompt examples across Korinek's six domains, with real LLM outputs and usefulness ratings Guide2EconRA (GitHub) Comprehensive resource collection for economics RAs — Python/R/Julia/Stata, causal inference, ML, reproducibility AEI — AI Tools for Economists Practical tool comparison (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, NotebookLM, Cursor) written for policy economists

Know a resource that should be here? Send a quick note — I'm always looking for what I've missed.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
Resources for thinking about AI in research and professional work more broadly.

Resource Why it's worth reading Simon Willison's Blog The most technically literate and honest AI blog. Simon builds tools and explains what works without hype. Claude Code projects on GitHub Community projects, extensions, and configurations tagged with "claude-code" on GitHub. r/ClaudeAI Active subreddit for Claude users. Good for troubleshooting and discovering new patterns. awesome-claude-code Curated index of Claude Code skills, hooks, slash commands, and CLAUDE.md patterns. The closest thing to a package manager catalog for the ecosystem. awesome-agent-skills 380+ curated skills from official dev teams (Anthropic, Vercel, Stripe, Cloudflare) and community. Cross-tool compatible. Quality-vetted. Claude Code Ultimate Guide 20,000+ lines, 16 specialized guides, 41 diagrams. The most comprehensive community reference for Claude Code architecture and workflows. CC BY-SA 4.0 licensed. LangChain Executive AI Assistant Production-ready Gmail-monitoring AI agent framework. Their "draft-only" pattern and human-in-the-loop review influenced how I built inbox triage.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Found a resource that should be here? Have a correction? Open an issue or start a discussion on GitHub.

docs.title: Why Claude Blattman switched to Codex
docs.text:
I started this site using Claude, but I now use Codex as my main workspace and coordinate Claude and other AIs through my Ask Agents and council skills.

The name has stayed (Codex Blattman doesn't quite roll off the tongue). Here's why I made Codex my main driver for now.

docs.title: I can work from my phone
docs.text:
I move between a desktop, a laptop, and my phone. Codex makes that much easier. If I remember a meeting while I'm at the gym, I can dictate what I need, ask it to gather the background, and come back to a briefing. My computer needs to be on and connected, but I don't need to be sitting in front of it.

By comparison, I've found Claude's mobile experience limited and clunky, at least with my setup. These apps change quickly. Here's how Codex's mobile connection works.

docs.title: The Codex app's preview pane is invaluable
docs.text: I can look at a PDF, Google Doc, or other document beside the chat and give feedback where I see the problem. Depending on the document, I can edit, comment, or annotate. It saves a surprising amount of explaining what I mean by “that bit halfway down.”

docs.title: There's no substitute for ChatGPT Deep Research
docs.text:
I also rely heavily on ChatGPT Deep Research in the browser. It's separate from Codex, but a big part of why I like the ChatGPT setup. For a thorough search, I haven't found anything that matches it. Even the strongest individual agents haven't been as careful or comprehensive. I still use agents, often several at once, to question the findings and work out what to do with them.

Confusingly, my /deep-research skill is a different thing. It sends several agents after the same question and pulls their findings together.

docs.title: My personal account gives me more flexibility
docs.text:
My university provides Claude at low cost to me, which is great, and it has been supportive of these tools. Its account comes with university-wide rules for connections and new features. My workflow also depends on personal accounts such as Gmail, and my own setup gives me more room to experiment, within limits I've set.

I still use Claude as one of the AIs on my councils.

My preference could change again in a few months. If your app works for you, keep using it. The approaches on this site travel well, and Different AI models explains how to bring other models into your work.

Updated November 2026.

docs.title: Write persistent instructions to your CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md file
docs.text:
A CLAUDE.md file is a personal instruction document that Claude Code reads automatically every time you start a session. It tells Claude who you are, how you work, what tools you use, and what you need help with.

Without it, every session starts fresh. With it, Claude begins each session already understanding your context.

Codex reads a file called AGENTS.md instead — same idea, different filename. If you use both apps, you want one file, not two that drift apart. How to do that is at the end of this page; everything between here and there applies to both.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A good CLAUDE.md file:

  • Saves time — No more repeating "I'm a researcher working on X using Y tools"
  • Improves responses — Claude tailors suggestions to your actual workflow and skill level
  • Reduces errors — When Claude knows where your files live, it gives relevant paths and suggestions
  • Compounds — As you refine the document, Claude gets better at helping you

The investment is small (20-30 minutes to start) and the payoff grows with every session.

docs.title: Single Computer
docs.text:
Claude Code looks for your CLAUDE.md here:

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

The ~ means your home folder. The .claude folder is hidden (folders starting with . are hidden by default).

To create it on Mac (mkdir -p creates a folder; ~ means your home directory): 

mkdir -p ~/.claude

To see hidden files in Finder: Press Cmd + Shift + .

docs.title: Multiple Computers (Recommended)
docs.text:
If you work across machines, store your CLAUDE.md in a synced folder and create a symlink:

A symlink is a shortcut — it makes a file appear in two places at once. ln -sf creates one. This lets you store the real file in a synced folder while Claude Code finds it in its expected location.

# Store the real file in your cloud sync folder
# (replace with your actual path — Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud, etc.)
mkdir -p ~/Documents/Claude-Settings

# Create the symlink so Claude Code finds it
mkdir -p ~/.claude
ln -sf ~/Documents/Claude-Settings/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

Repeat the symlink step on each computer. Now your CLAUDE.md syncs automatically.

Not sure the symlink worked?

In the app's message box, type: I set up the symlink but I'm not sure it worked. Can you verify it's connected properly? Press Enter. Claude can check the symlink and tell you if it's pointing to the right file.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
Copy this template and fill in the sections relevant to you. Delete any sections that don't apply.

# Claude Context: [Your Name]

## Who I Am

[1-2 sentences about your role.]

## My Primary Work

- [Main responsibility 1]
- [Main responsibility 2]
- [Main responsibility 3]

## Tools and Software

| Tool | What I Use It For | Where Files Live |
|------|-------------------|------------------|
| [e.g., Stata] | [e.g., Statistical analysis] | [e.g., ~/Research/] |
| [e.g., Google Docs] | [e.g., Writing, collaboration] | [e.g., Google Drive] |

## Where My Files Are Stored

- **Working files:** [e.g., ~/Dropbox/Research/]
- **Data:** [e.g., ~/Box/Data/ — note if Claude can't access]
- **Code:** [e.g., GitHub repos]
- **Shared docs:** [e.g., Google Drive shared folders]

## What I Need Help With

- [Use case 1]
- [Use case 2]
- [Use case 3]

## My Skill Level

- **Coding:** [e.g., "Intermediate in Stata, beginner in R"]
- **Statistics:** [e.g., "Comfortable with regression, learning causal inference"]
- **Command line:** [e.g., "Beginner — explain commands before running them"]

## How I Prefer to Work

- [e.g., "Explain reasoning when suggesting code changes"]
- [e.g., "Ask before modifying files outside my project"]
- [e.g., "Be concise unless I ask for detail"]

## Current Projects

| Project | My Role | Current Phase |
|---------|---------|---------------|
| [Name] | [Role] | [Phase] |

Let Claude help you fill it in.

In the app's message box, type something like: Help me fill out my CLAUDE.md. I'm a political science professor who studies conflict and development. Press Enter. Claude will ask follow-up questions and draft sections for you.

docs.title: Underdeveloped (Too Vague)
docs.text:
# About Me
I'm a researcher. I do data analysis and help with projects.
I use Stata and R.

This doesn't give Claude enough to work with. What kind of projects? Where are files stored? What's your skill level?

docs.title: Good (Specific and Actionable)
docs.text:
# Claude Context: Jamie Rivera

## Who I Am
Predoctoral research assistant at a policy school, working on field
experiments studying education interventions in East Africa.

## My Primary Work
- Cleaning and merging survey data (primarily in Stata)
- Running analysis and creating tables/figures for working papers
- Managing project documentation and IRB protocols
- Coordinating with field teams via WhatsApp and email

## Tools and Software

| Tool | What I Use It For | Where Files Live |
|------|-------------------|------------------|
| Stata 18 | Primary analysis | Local + GitHub |
| R | Visualization | Local + GitHub |
| GitHub | Version control | github.com/[org] |
| Box | Sensitive data (PII) | Institutional Box |
| Google Docs | Drafts, collaboration | Shared drives |

## Where My Files Are Stored
- Code and analysis: ~/Dropbox/Research/[project]/code/
- Non-sensitive data: ~/Dropbox/Research/[project]/data/
- Sensitive data: Institutional Box only — Claude cannot access

## What I Need Help With
- Debugging Stata code and improving efficiency
- Writing R visualization scripts
- Drafting professional emails
- Understanding new statistical methods
- Organizing project documentation

## My Skill Level
- Stata: Advanced (4 years)
- R: Intermediate (comfortable, still learning tidyverse)
- Python: Beginner
- Git: Intermediate (basic workflow, less comfortable with branches)
- Terminal: Comfortable with basics

## How I Prefer to Work
- Include comments explaining code sections
- Ask before modifying or deleting files
- Explain errors before giving fixes
- I use dictation, so prompts may be conversational

## Current Projects
| Project | My Role | Current Phase |
|---------|---------|---------------|
| Education RCT | Lead RA | Analysis + writing |
| Youth Survey | Data management | Survey programming |

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Start minimal, then expand. Your first version should take 20 minutes. Add detail as you discover what's useful.

Be specific about file locations. "I use Dropbox" is less useful than "~/Dropbox/Research/ with subfolders per project containing /code/, /data/, and /docs/."

Include your skill level. A beginner needs explanations; an expert wants efficiency. Don't oversell your skills — Claude will calibrate its responses wrong.

Update when things change. New project? New tool? Update your CLAUDE.md. A stale document is worse than a minimal one.

docs.title: Test It
docs.text:
After creating your CLAUDE.md, start Claude Code and ask:

"What do you know about me and my work?"

Claude should reference information from your file. If it doesn't, check:

  1. File location: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
  2. File name: Must be exactly CLAUDE.md
  3. File contents: Open it and verify it's not empty

docs.title: Model Choice
docs.text:
Claude Code defaults to the Sonnet 4.6 model, which is fast and capable for most tasks. For complex work — long-form writing, nuanced analysis, multi-step reasoning — consider switching to Opus 4.6:

/model opus

Opus 4.6 is more capable but uses more tokens per response (higher cost, faster usage against plan limits). This setting applies to the current session only. Switch back with /model sonnet.

docs.title: Advanced: Project-Specific CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
In addition to your global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, you can create a CLAUDE.md in any project folder. Claude reads both when you start a session in that directory.

How they work together:

File Location Purpose Global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Who you are — role, preferences, contact info, working style Project my-project/.claude/CLAUDE.md This specific project — team, tools, conventions, file paths

Claude loads the global file first, then the project file. Project instructions can override or extend global ones.

my-project/
├── .claude/
│   └── CLAUDE.md    ← project-specific instructions
├── data/
├── code/
└── docs/

This is useful when you work on multiple projects with different conventions, team members, or tools.

What goes in your CLAUDE.md is sent to the API

Everything in your CLAUDE.md files is included in every conversation with Claude Code. This is how Claude knows about you and your projects. The data is covered by Anthropic's API data policy. Avoid including passwords, API keys, or information you wouldn't want transmitted to a cloud service.

docs.title: Voice & Writing Style
docs.text:
If AI output never quite sounds like your writing — too formal, too hedgy, full of words you'd never use — a voice file fixes that. It's a document that captures your actual writing patterns: sentence structure, vocabulary preferences, a ban list of AI-isms, and annotated examples.

The simplest implementation: save your core voice file to ~/.claude/rules/ and it auto-loads every session, just like other rule files. No @import needed for the fundamentals.

~/.claude/rules/core-voice.md    ← auto-loads every session

For context-specific registers (proposal voice vs. email voice), load those on demand through skills or @voice/ imports in project-level CLAUDE.md files.

Teaching AI your voice — build the voice file step by step, with a fill-in template

docs.title: If you use Codex too: AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Claude reads CLAUDE.md. Codex reads AGENTS.md. The contents are interchangeable — the only difference is the filename each app looks for.

Two copies is the obvious approach and the wrong one: they drift, and the day they disagree you won't know which app read which. Make one file the real one and the other a pointer to it.

Ask your agent to do it, in the folder where the file lives:

Make AGENTS.md a symlink to CLAUDE.md in this folder, so both apps read the same file.

A symlink is a stand-in that points at the real file — open either name and you get the same content. Edit CLAUDE.md and Codex sees the change immediately, because there is only one file.

Which one should be the real file?

Whichever app you use more. If you mostly work in Claude, keep CLAUDE.md real and point AGENTS.md at it, as above. The arrangement is symmetrical; what matters is that exactly one of them holds the text.

The same pattern works for the global file — Claude's at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, Codex's at ~/.codex/AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Downloadable Template & Real Example
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md Template — The starter file. Fill in the blanks.
  • A Real CLAUDE.md — Annotated — My actual production CLAUDE.md (sanitized), showing what a mature configuration looks like after months of iteration. Study this when you're ready to level up.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
With your CLAUDE.md in place:

  1. Connect external services — Give Claude access to email, docs, and calendar
  2. Explore skills — Download tools that automate common workflows

Yay, my agent knows who I am!

docs.title: Turn repeatable workflows into skills
docs.text: Skills save a repeatable way of working in Claude Code or Codex. Each maintained skill lives in its own folder, with instructions in SKILL.md and any references or scripts beside it. This page shows how to build one from work you already do.

docs.title: 1. Notice the Pattern
docs.text:
