The best skills come from noticing what you do repeatedly. Pay attention to:

  • Prompts you type out more than twice
  • Multi-step workflows you walk Claude through manually
  • Tasks where you always provide the same context or constraints

docs.title: 2. Do It Manually First
docs.text:
Before formalizing anything, do the task through normal conversation. Repeat it enough to see which instructions help. Each time, notice:

  • What instructions you give
  • What the agent gets right and wrong
  • What you have to correct or clarify
  • What context you always have to re-provide

docs.title: 3. Write the Skill
docs.text:
Create a folder named after the skill, with a SKILL.md file inside. Start the file with metadata that says what it does and when to use it:

---
name: your-skill
description: Describe the task this skill handles and when to use it.
---

# Your skill

[1-2 sentence description of what this skill does and when to use it]

## Inputs

Read the user's accompanying request for:
- [The details the user can provide]

## Instructions

### Step 1: [First action]
[What the agent should do]

### Step 2: [Second action]
[What the agent should do]

### Step 3: [Output]
[What the agent should show the user]

For a project-specific skill, use the folder for your app:

App File inside your project Claude Code .claude/skills/your-skill/SKILL.md Codex .agents/skills/your-skill/SKILL.md

The name in the metadata should match the folder name. A simple skill needs only SKILL.md. Add references/, scripts/ or assets/ only when it needs supporting material, and keep paths relative to the skill folder. See the Agent Skills specification.

Open a fresh session in that project. Check that the app lists the intended skill. Invoke /your-skill in Claude Code or select $your-skill in Codex, and try a real task. If the skill uses a reference, check that the agent actually reads it.

Older Claude Code commands in .claude/commands/ still work in that app. For new skills, use the folder format. Before replacing an existing command, back it up and preserve its customizations. Check for a same-named installed skill or plugin rather than assuming the new file will be the one that runs.

docs.title: 4. Test and Iterate
docs.text:
Run the skill. It won't be right the first time. Common issues:

  • Too verbose — Add constraints: "Keep output under 200 words"
  • Missing context — Add more instructions or @ references
  • Wrong format — Specify exact output structure
  • Doesn't handle edge cases — Add error handling sections

docs.title: 5. Stabilize
docs.text:
Once the skill works reliably:

  • Add a version header (*v1.0 — date — description*)
  • Add argument documentation
  • Add error handling for common failures
  • Test with different inputs

docs.title: Arguments ($ARGUMENTS)
docs.text:
Explain which inputs the skill accepts. Claude Code can substitute the text after a slash command through $ARGUMENTS. In Codex, describe how to read the user's accompanying request rather than relying on that Claude-specific substitution.

Common patterns: 

## Arguments
`$ARGUMENTS` can include:
- *(none)* — default behavior
- `quick` — abbreviated output
- `file:path` — specify a file
- `depth:light/standard/deep` — control thoroughness

docs.title: Supporting references
docs.text:
Keep reference material beside the instructions and tell the agent when to read it:

## Reference Files
Before drafting, read `references/style-guide.md` and
`references/voice-rules.md` relative to this skill folder.

Use for: - Shared rules across multiple skills - Style guides or voice preferences — see Teaching AI your voice for a complete example - Configuration that changes independently

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Anticipate what goes wrong:

## Error Handling
- **No input provided:** Show usage example and exit
- **File not found:** Report the missing path and suggest alternatives
- **MCP not available:** Explain what's missing and offer to proceed without it

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
Be explicit about what the user sees:

### Output

Display:
| Column 1 | Column 2 |
|----------|----------|
| [data]   | [data]   |

Then ask: "Apply these changes? Or provide feedback to adjust."

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
One skill, one job. A skill that tries to do three things will be fragile and hard to improve. Three focused skills are better.

Match complexity to task. A 5-line skill for formatting a quick note is fine. A 200-line skill for comprehensive plan review is also fine. Don't over-engineer simple tasks or under-specify complex ones.

Default to action. Skills should do something useful with no arguments. Make the zero-argument case the most common workflow.

Fail gracefully. When something goes wrong (missing file, MCP not connected), the skill should explain what happened and suggest a fix — not crash silently.

Version and document. Add a version header and argument documentation. Future-you will thank present-you.

docs.title: Patterns to Steal
docs.text:
These patterns appear in well-designed skills:

Pattern What It Does Example Flags parsing Parse $ARGUMENTS for named flags depth:deep, file:path, quick Phased execution Multi-step with user checkpoints Discover → Plan → Implement Depth calibration Adjust thoroughness based on context Light / Standard / Deep Critic stance Explicitly shift Claude's role "You are now the critic, not the planner" Output templates Fixed format for consistent results Status dashboard, review format Iteration gates Pause for user feedback before continuing "Apply these changes? Or adjust?"

See Patterns for the full catalog.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agents vs Skills — When to use a subagent instead
  • Patterns — Reusable design patterns and quality checklist
  • skills on GitHub — Study existing skills as examples
  • Skill Design Patterns — Downloadable reference with archetypes, quality checklist, and performance logging conventions (February 2026)

I built a skill!

docs.title: Connect your apps
docs.text:
A project folder gives the agent your local files. Connections let it work with the information you keep elsewhere: email, calendars, shared documents, and messages. Instead of copying a thread into the chat, you can ask it to find the thread and use it.

As always, ask your AI to help you set this up. Start with a task and the app that holds the information you need. You can add more connections as your work calls for them.

docs.title: 1. Tell the agent what you want to connect
docs.text:
Open your project in Claude Code or Codex and ask:

Help me connect [app] so you can use it in this project. Check what is already available, do the setup you can, and walk me through anything I need to do myself.

A connection may let the agent read information, make changes, or both. Ask it to explain the access the connection requests. You will usually need to sign in yourself.

Where to find the connections yourself ClaudeCodex

Open Customize → Connectors, find the service, and select Connect or Install. Follow the sign-in prompts. See the Claude connector guide for the current controls.

Open the desktop app's Plugins tab, find the service, and install its plugin. Connect the account when prompted, then start a new chat to use it. The OpenAI plugin guide explains the available connections and controls.

On a university or company account, an administrator may need to enable the connection first. Ask your agent to help distinguish an account restriction from an unfinished sign-in.

I've connected an app my work needs.

docs.title: 2. Try it on something you can recognize
docs.text:
Ask for a specific email, event, or document so you can tell whether the connection works:

Find my latest email thread with [name] about [topic]. Summarize what we agreed and link to the thread.

For documents, try: “Find the latest proposal for [project] and tell me what still needs work.” If you have more than one account, say which one you mean.

My agent found the right material through the connection.

docs.title: 3. Give it a task that uses the connected information
docs.text:
Now ask for the result you actually need. For example:

Help me prepare for my meeting with [name]. Read our recent emails and the proposal in this project. What decisions do we need to make, and what should I ask? Save a short meeting brief here.

You can bring several sources into the same request once they are connected. The meeting workflow shows how to turn that preparation into follow-up afterward.

I've used connected information on a real task.

docs.title: 4. Fix a connection when it stops working
docs.text:
Often the next step is simply signing in again. Ask the agent to check:

The connection to [app] isn't working. Help me diagnose it, walk me through any sign-in I need to repeat, and test that you can retrieve something afterward.

You can manage or disconnect accounts in the app's connection settings. If a service is missing from the directory, ask your AI to investigate the supported options before building anything custom.

What if there is no built-in connection?

MCP is a standard that lets an AI use tools supplied by another service. Many connectors already use it behind the scenes. A service may offer an official custom connector, or there may be a plugin that supplies the connection.

Ask: “Is there a supported connection for [app] in the AI I'm using? If there isn't, what is the simplest way to work with its information?” Sometimes opening the service in the agent's browser or exporting a document is enough.

I know how to ask for help when a connection needs attention.

docs.title: Bring research tools into your workflow
docs.text:
Add a tool when you have a job for it. For research, two useful examples are a notebook for working through sources and a reference manager for keeping them organized.

Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) lets you collect sources in a notebook and ask questions about them. You can bring the resulting notes or report back into your project. See the notebook guide and Google's introduction. Using a separate research notebook does not by itself connect it to your agent.

Zotero organizes references, attached PDFs, and notes. If you already use it, ask your agent how to work with the library you have. It can investigate an available connector or help you export the relevant references and files. The Zotero guide explains its library and export features.

I keep my research in [app]. Help me use the relevant sources for [project]. Check whether you can connect to it. If not, help me bring over the files or notes we need.

Dictation and meeting transcription have their own guides. Start with the tools you already use and add others when they help with a real task.

docs.title: Set up rules and guidelines
docs.text:
Your instruction file says who you are and where things live. Rules are the other half: what to do, and what never to do. They apply to everything, so you write them once instead of repeating yourself every session.

The difference matters. "My drafts live in ~/Projects" is context. "Never send an email without showing me the draft first" is a rule.

docs.title: Start with the ones you've already repeated
docs.text:
Don't sit down to write a rulebook. Watch for the moment you correct the agent twice for the same thing — that correction is your first rule. Mine came from being irritated, not from planning:

  • Meeting notes go at the top of the file, newest first.
  • Never create a mail filter without asking. Filters run when I'm not there.
  • Drafts only for anything that leaves my machine.

Three rules you actually use beat thirty you aspired to.

docs.title: Split them once there are more than a dozen
docs.text:
A single file of forty rules gets skimmed. At that point, break them into topic files — one for how you write, one for how projects are organised, one per integration that has a quirk — and have the instruction file point at them. The agent loads the relevant one when the subject comes up.

Keep the genuinely load-bearing ones inline, where they can't be missed:

Sending email: show me the draft. Never send directly.
Meeting logs: newest entry at the top.

A real annotated example

docs.title: What makes a rule hold
docs.text:
This is the part that surprised me, and it runs against instinct.

Shouting makes rules weaker, not stronger. CRITICAL: YOU MUST NEVER reads as emphasis to you and as noise to the model. When everything is critical, nothing is. Strip the ceremony and the real constraints start standing out again.

Say what to do, not only what to avoid. "Write in flowing prose with no headers or bullets" works better than "don't use markdown". When you do have to forbid something, pair the ban with the thing you want instead.

Use action verbs, not adjectives. "Be thorough" is empty. "Compare this against the pre-registration and list every discrepancy" is a rule that can actually be followed — or visibly not followed, which is just as useful.

The full version of this argument

docs.title: Rules are not a safety system
docs.text:
A rule is an instruction the agent will almost always follow. It is not a mechanism that prevents anything.

If the consequence of a rule being missed is real — mail sent, a file overwritten, data leaving your machine — put a permission behind it as well, not just a sentence. The permissions step is what actually stops an action; rules shape behaviour inside whatever permissions allow.

That distinction is the same one the newcomer checklist makes about plan mode: asking for a plan is a request, and the mode is the thing that enforces it.

docs.title: Revisit them when they stop earning their place
docs.text:
Rules accumulate. Some were written for a quirk that has since been fixed, and a rule that no longer applies is just context being burned on every session.

Keeping your setup current

My agent is now ruled.

docs.title: Teaching AI your voice
docs.text:
A draft can be accurate and still sound wrong. It may explain too little, sound too formal for the reader, or bury the decision under polished paragraphs. A useful voice pack captures those choices and, most importantly, helps your AI sound more like you, the human.

Start a voice project. Give it a name and a home in your app, just as you would any other project. It will hold your writing samples and two kinds of guidance: a core voice guide for the habits that stay consistent across your writing, and separate guides for different kinds of writing, such as email and long-form prose. Together, these make up your voice pack.

The starting point is gathering basic evidence so the AI sounds a little bit like you. Over time, it should sound a lot more like you. That comes from correcting it on real work. Build the pack here, then set up the system that learns from your edits.

Ask your AI to help you build it. Open a local Claude Code or Codex session and start with:

Walk me through the voice pack guide at claudeblattman.com. Ask me for the inputs you need first, then help me build it.

Congratulations! You now have an AI converging towards you. Page two shows how to make your corrections useful next time.

docs.title: 1. Start a voice project and point it at your corpus
docs.text:
Create a folder and open it as a project in Claude Code or Codex. If you need the steps, use the project setup in the first-session guide.

The first step is to build a collection of pieces you’ve written and would still stand behind. I refer to this collection as my corpus and name the folder corpus accordingly. Because I do so many different kinds of writing, and they all sound different, I organize my corpus into subcategories of writing. For example:

My voice/
└── corpus/
    ├── emails/
    │   ├── README.md
    │   └── team-update.txt
    ├── proposals/
    │   ├── README.md
    │   └── grant-proposal.docx
    └── op-eds/
        ├── README.md
        └── published-column.pdf

Alternatively, you could leave writing in its existing project folders. Ask the agent to make a corpus-index.md in your voice project that records the file paths and the same audience notes described below. The important thing is that it can find and read the sources.

For emails, ask the agent to start with a random sample of 100 sent messages. Emails are so varied that a handful of favorites may miss much of your writing style. A random sample gives the agent a broader starting point across recipients, purposes, thread lengths, and how much the reader already knows. Look at what it found and add examples of any important kind of email it missed.

Ask the agent to help gather email samples

I had agents take random samples of hundreds of emails. If your agent has an email connection, it can do the gathering for you:

Help me build my email corpus. Ask me what date range to use, then select a random sample of 100 sent messages I wrote, or all available messages if there are fewer. Keep my words separate from quoted replies and signatures, but retain enough thread context to understand the message. Save the samples and source references in my voice project. Tell me which audiences and kinds of email are represented and which seem missing. Flag uncertain authorship and ask me about AI assistance you cannot establish.

If it cannot access your email, give it an export or a set of messages to work from.

I've built my corpus.

docs.title: 2. Explain what each sample was trying to do
docs.text:
Ask the agent to help you write a short guide to the samples in your corpus. Each subfolder’s README.md tells it when to draw on those samples: who you were writing to, your relationship, and what the writing needed to accomplish.

Create a README file for each corpus subfolder with a short entry for each sample. Note the filename, audience and relationship, and purpose. The goal is to teach the voice pack how and when to draw writing guidance from each sample based on what the agent is trying to write from scratch. Take a first pass, then ask me for context you can't establish from the files. Don't make guesses.

Read its first pass and fill in the gaps. “This person already knew the background” can explain why an email was brief. Identify your sections of collaborative writing and label AI-assisted drafts so the agent knows whose words it is learning from.

Using a chatbot?

Attach the samples to your message. Ask the chatbot to read them and build the README notes, using the prompt above. Then use the samples and notes to build the voice pack by following the rest of this guide.

Once it is built, put the guidance from CORE_VOICE.md, EMAIL_VOICE.md, LONG_FORM_VOICE.md, and your other guides into the chatbot’s project-level instructions. Attach your individual samples and README notes as project-level context.

My samples have notes explaining their audience and purpose.

docs.title: 3. Let the AI analyze them, then check its reading
docs.text:
Ask the agent what stays consistent across your writing and what changes with the audience or type of piece. Check whether its description sounds like you, and have it show you the passages behind its conclusions:

Read these samples, their notes, and help me describe how I write. Identify habits shared across my writing and differences specific to emails, long-form prose, proposals, or other types in my corpus. Quote the passages behind your observations. Look at how I open, explain my reasoning, handle uncertainty, address the reader, organize the material, and end. Notice tone, rhythm and amount of detail too.

Separate patterns that belong in my core voice guide from choices that belong in a writing-type guide or seem idiosyncratic to one individual piece.

Read the analysis as yourself. “I do that in grant proposals, but not in emails” is a useful correction. So is “That sentence is from my co-author.” Tell it when a pattern is accidental, or when the explanation misses why you made a choice.

I've checked the analysis against my writing and corrected what it missed.

docs.title: 4. Build your core and writing-type guides
docs.text:
My pack starts with CORE_VOICE.md, which holds the voice properties that apply across my writing. Then it has separate guides for email, proposals, public writing, long-form prose, and other kinds of work. You can use the same structure with just the types you need:

My voice/
├── CORE_VOICE.md        Shared voice across writing types
├── EMAIL_VOICE.md       Emails
├── LONG_FORM_VOICE.md   Books and extended essays, if needed
├── [OTHER]_VOICE.md     Specific guides as needed
└── corpus/             Samples and their README notes

The core holds what stays consistent—your way of explaining an argument, handling uncertainty, or addressing the reader. Each writing-type guide explains what changes: how much background to give, how to organize the piece, or how formal to be.

Using the analysis and my corrections, build CORE_VOICE.md for preferences that apply across my writing. Create separate guides for the writing types I use, such as EMAIL_VOICE.md and LONG_FORM_VOICE.md. Keep shared guidance in the core and the differences in the relevant guide. Explain when each guide applies, including any specific exceptions to a core default. Include a few unchanged passages from my samples in each relevant guide, with a short note on the audience, purpose, and what the example illustrates. Use my samples and decisions, not someone else's personal writing rules. Flag anything I still need to decide.

You can include a do-not-use list of words, phrases, or formatting choices. My core guide calls this its ‘Anti-AI Vocabulary’ list. The pack should also explain what good writing sounds like for you. Your core guide can change as you learn more about your preferences.

Prefer a starting template? Give your agent the Voice Pack Template and ask it to adapt its useful sections into the core and writing-type guides above, using your samples and decisions.

Examples belong in the guides from the start. A short note can explain what to borrow from a passage: how you introduce a disagreement, how much context you give, or how you make a request friendly and direct.

I've built my core and writing-type guides, with examples.

docs.title: 5. Make your voice pack the default
docs.text:
Now make this a standing instruction so you don't have to ask for your voice pack every time. My setup already directs the agent to the guides when it drafts or edits my writing. The agent should know to use them from those saved instructions.

Ask it to add a short pointer to your personal, global instructions, which apply across projects. A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md inside just the voice folder would only cover that project.

ClaudeCodex 
Make my core voice and other writing guides the default when you draft or edit writing for me. Add a standing instruction to my personal CLAUDE.md. Always read and use my core voice, and use the relevant writing guide when needed. Preserve the other instructions unless they directly contradict my core voice. If they do, reconcile the conflicting writing instructions and flag what changed.

Claude Code's personal CLAUDE.md applies across projects.

Make my core voice and other writing guides the default when you draft or edit writing for me. Add a standing instruction to my personal AGENTS.md. Always read and use my core voice, and use the relevant writing guide when needed. Preserve the other instructions unless they directly contradict my core voice. If they do, reconcile the conflicting writing instructions and flag what changed.

Codex's personal AGENTS.md supplies defaults across projects.

If you write in both apps, do this once in each. On another computer, ask the agent to connect its personal instructions to the voice folder there too.

My agent has a standing instruction to use my voice pack when writing for me.

docs.title: 6. Try it on a real writing task
docs.text:
Open a new session in a project where you have writing to do. With the standing instruction in place, you can make an ordinary request. For example:

Draft an email to [recipient] and cc [colleague] about [topic]. Use the notes in this project. I want them to [next step].

You shouldn't need to name the voice files again. If the result sounds wrong, ask the agent to check whether it used your saved voice instructions, then explain what you want changed.

Correct the writing. You can rewrite it yourself or explain the change aloud. “Make it shorter” is less helpful than “They already know the background. Keep the reason for the delay, then make the question easy to find.” Notice how much editing remains before you would send it.

Having trouble explaining what sounds wrong?

Try a comparison. I’ve asked the AI to show me a few paragraphs and A/B test which version I think is better. You can ask for two versions of the same passage, with the same facts and audience, then explain which you prefer and why. This can help you put a preference into words. You do not need to run a series of tests before using the pack.

I get into the process of learning from your feedback in more detail on the next page.

I've used the pack on a real draft and corrected what mattered.

docs.title: Agents vs Skills
docs.text:
An agent is an AI worker that uses a model and tools to carry out tasks. Claude Code and Codex are agent products; models such as GPT-6.1 Sol power the workers. A subagent is a separate worker started by the main agent. This page uses “agents” for those subagents.

Claude Code has two main building blocks: skills (slash commands that run in the main conversation) and agents (subprocesses that run in a separate context). Choosing the right one matters for reliability and quality.

docs.title: The Key Difference
docs.text: Dimension Skill Agent Context Runs in the main conversation with full history Runs in a fresh context — no prior conversation User interaction Can ask questions, show drafts, get feedback Returns a single result when done Memory Sees everything discussed so far Sees only what you explicitly pass to it Bias May be influenced by prior conversation ("self-bias") Fresh perspective — evaluates only what's written Speed Instant (already in context) Slower (starts a new process)

docs.title: When to Use a Skill
docs.text:
Skills work best when the task:

  • Needs conversation context — The task builds on what you've already discussed
  • Requires user input — You need to answer questions or make choices mid-workflow
  • Is a workflow — Multi-step processes with user checkpoints
  • Modifies state — Writing files, sending emails, updating docs

Examples: - /done — Captures decisions from the current session (needs conversation history) - /council — Coordinates independent agents using the task context - /setup-project-management — Multi-phase setup with user decisions at each stage

docs.title: When to Use an Agent
docs.text:
Agents work best when the task:

  • Benefits from fresh eyes — Review, critique, or evaluation tasks where prior context creates blind spots
  • Can run in parallel — Multiple evaluations or analyses that don't depend on each other
  • Needs isolation — You don't want the task polluting your main conversation context
  • Has a clear input and output — "Here's a file, give me a review" rather than "let's work through this together"

Examples: - Writing review — A fresh context evaluates the prose without knowing "what you meant" - Methodology review — Catches issues that the session that wrote the paper might miss - Parallel research — Launch 3 agents to investigate different approaches simultaneously

docs.title: Agent Debates: Multiple Perspectives on the Same Problem
docs.text:
One of the most powerful uses of agents is getting them to argue with each other. Instead of a single review, you set up multiple agents with different expertise or perspectives and let them debate your data, your plan, or your design.

Qualitative researchers analyzing pilot field data

We'd just finished a pilot — seven university students visited low-income neighborhoods in Bogota they'd never been to. We had memos the students wrote, open-ended survey responses, and quantitative survey data. Normally, a first pass through qualitative data like this takes days.

I set up two agents as qualitative researchers from different traditions — one grounded theory, one thematic analysis — and gave them the anonymized memos, open-ended responses, and quantitative results. Their tasks: produce an initial interpretive report, compare the qualitative themes against the survey patterns, and draft best practices for a post-pilot debriefing interview guide.

Twenty minutes later, we had intelligent first glimpses across the whole dataset. The agents flagged where the memos contradicted the survey numbers — students reported feeling safer in the quantitative data, but their memos focused on discovery and surprise rather than safety. They caught that one survey item moved in an unexpected direction and proposed interview questions to probe it. Each agent emphasized different things depending on their methodological lens, which told us what to pay attention to when we went back to read carefully.

It didn't replace our own close reading. But it meant we had quick analysis and multiple perspectives immediately — a starting point for reflection rather than starting from scratch. We then used our own custom LLMs for the deeper qualitative analysis.

Behavioral economists critiquing a research design

For the same project, I asked Claude to impersonate three close colleagues of mine — Alex Imas, Leonardo Bursztyn, and Richard Thaler, all behavioral economists at UChicago — and debate our study design.

"Imas" reframed our entire finding: the treatment wasn't reducing prejudice, it was shifting students' reference point for public goods. They'd seen parks in low-income areas that were better than parks in their own wealthy neighborhoods. That's not attitude change — it's a recalibration of what they thought was normal.

"Bursztyn" was blunt: self-reported attitudes are "essentially worthless" in this context. Students know the right answer. He proposed three revealed-preference measures — including offering students a restaurant gift card redeemable in either their own neighborhood or the one they visited. The choice reveals what they actually believe, not what they'll say on a survey.

"Thaler" argued we were framing the whole study wrong. This isn't a "contact hypothesis" paper — it's a study about choice architecture. The cable car that takes you to the neighborhood is the intervention. His proposed title: "The Blank Map: How Elites Think About Neighborhoods They've Never Visited."

Each persona saw a different paper in the same data. The debate generated a table of nine new measures to add to the full study — none of which were in our original design.

The pattern: give agents distinct identities (methodological traditions, named colleagues, opposing stakeholders) and let the disagreements surface assumptions you hadn't examined. The value isn't in any single perspective — it's in where they clash.

docs.title: The Self-Bias Problem
docs.text:
This is the most important reason to use agents for review tasks.

When Claude writes something in a conversation and then you ask it to review that same thing, it has a systematic bias toward finding its own work acceptable. It "knows what it meant" even if the text is ambiguous. It may not question assumptions it made earlier.

An agent running in a fresh context doesn't have this problem. It evaluates only what's on the page — like handing your draft to a colleague who wasn't in the room when you wrote it.

Rule of thumb: If you're asking Claude to critique something it helped create, use an agent.

docs.title: Agent File Format
docs.text:
Agents are markdown files saved in ~/.claude/agents/:

---
name: Agent Name
description: What this agent does
model: sonnet
tools:
  - Read
  - Glob
  - Grep
---

# Agent Name

[Instructions for the agent]

## Review Dimensions
[What to evaluate]

## Output Format
[How to structure the response]

The YAML frontmatter specifies: - model — Which Claude model to use (sonnet is cost-effective for most review tasks) - tools — Which tools the agent can access (limit to what it needs)

docs.title: Launching Agents
docs.text:
From within Claude Code:

"Launch the writing reviewer agent on ~/Documents/paper-draft.md"

Claude Code reads the agent file, starts a subprocess, passes the specified files, and returns the result to your main conversation.

You can launch multiple agents simultaneously:

"Launch both the writing reviewer and methodology reviewer on this paper draft"

They run in parallel and return independent assessments.

docs.title: Design Guidance
docs.text:
Scenario Use Why Reviewing your own draft Agent Avoids self-bias Multi-step workflow with decisions Skill Needs user interaction Parallel evaluations Multiple agents Independent fresh contexts Task needs conversation history Skill Agent doesn't see prior context Heavy task that would bloat context Agent Keeps main conversation lean One-time setup or configuration Skill Needs to read/write files and ask questions

For a more detailed decision framework with additional examples, see the Agents vs Skills Decision Guide (February 2026).

docs.title: Chatbots done right
docs.text:
A chatbot is useful for more than looking up an answer. Give it a draft to improve, a set of options to compare, or a problem to help you work through. The value often comes in the conversation after the first answer.

This guide works in an ordinary browser chat. If your workplace restricts agents, start with the chatbot it allows. For personal projects and the bigger picture, see Get ahead of the curve.

docs.title: Choose a model that fits the job
docs.text:
Look at the model or reasoning options available in your approved tool. A quick rewrite may not need the same model as a difficult analysis. For work that needs careful comparison, synthesis, or judgment, try a more capable reasoning option and compare the results on your actual task.

More capable models may take longer or use more of your allowance. Model names, defaults, and access change; you don't need to memorize a ranking or buy the most expensive subscription before you start. The useful question is whether the result improves enough to matter.

docs.title: Tell it what it needs to know
docs.text:
A generic request usually gets a generic answer. Give the chatbot enough information to understand your situation: what you're trying to achieve, who the result is for, what's already decided, and what would make its answer unusable.

“Help me plan a trip” leaves almost everything to guesswork. Try:

We're planning a five-day family trip in October. We want one base,
short outings, and something to do if it rains. One person loves
museums; another gets restless indoors. We won't rent a car.

Suggest three kinds of destination to investigate. Compare the
trade-offs for each person. Ask if a missing detail would materially
change your suggestions. Don't make up prices or availability.

The same habit helps at work. With an approved tool and material you're allowed to use, a brief might start: “I coordinate a small research team. I'm preparing a one-page update for a nontechnical funder. They need the decisions and delays, not a literature review.” Your role, audience, and purpose all change what a useful answer looks like.

You can say this out loud. A messy explanation with the relevant details is often more useful than a beautifully formatted prompt with none of them. If you're stuck, ask: “What do you need to know to help me with this?”

docs.title: Give it a clear job and a usable output
docs.text:
Specify what you want back. A comparison table? A ready-to-send email? Three questions to ask a contractor? A critique of the weakest part of a draft?

Compare “Help me with an update” with “Turn these approved notes into a 200-word update for our funder. Lead with the decision needed, then progress and delays. Mark missing dates rather than inventing them.” The second request defines a result you can assess.

A useful request covers context, task, format, and constraints. You rarely need a long template. For a bigger job, the prompting guide shows how to put those pieces together—or have the AI do the formatting for you.

Give it permission to disagree: “If none of these options meets my requirements, say so.” That invites useful criticism, though it doesn't guarantee the criticism is right.

docs.title: Work through the answer together
docs.text:
Treat the first response as something to react to. Tell it which part works and which part doesn't. Specific feedback gives the next attempt a direction:

The comparison is useful, but you've ignored the no-car constraint.
Recheck each option against it and remove anything that depends
on driving. Keep the table and explain what changed.

For writing, “less formal” is a start. “Keep my opening, cut the second paragraph in half, and replace the abstract claims with the example I gave you” is much easier to act on.

A short exchange can improve one draft in stages:

You: What are the two weakest parts of this introduction?
AI:  [Identifies an unsupported claim and a confusing second paragraph.]
You: Rewrite paragraph two using the example in my notes.
AI:  [Produces a revision.]
You: The structure works, but the tone is too formal. Keep my opening
     sentence and use shorter sentences in the rest.
AI:  [Revises again.]
You: Now apply those changes to paragraph four. Keep the figures as given.

Stay in the same conversation while you refine the same piece of work. When the task changes, or the conversation has become tangled in abandoned approaches, start a new chat with a short handoff:

Summarize what the next chat needs: the goal, current decisions,
constraints, useful sources, unresolved questions, and next step.
Separate confirmed facts from ideas we haven't checked.

Read that summary before reusing it. A handoff can carry a mistake forward just as easily as a useful decision.

docs.title: Save the context you keep repeating
docs.text:
For recurring work, keep a short file of stable preferences and instructions. Put it in a chatbot Project if your account supports that, or paste it into a new chat when you need it.

Keep three things distinct:

  • General preferences: how much detail you like, how you want feedback, and your preferred writing style.
  • Project context: the relevant people, goals, constraints, reference files, and decisions.
  • Today's request: the particular draft, trip dates, question, or output you need now.

For example, a Grant writing project's standing instructions might say:

I write proposals for nontechnical foundation readers.
Lead with the claim and the evidence for it. Use direct language.
Flag unsupported statements and missing numbers; don't fill them in.
Keep the funder's priorities and the current proposal in the source
files. Ask which proposal we're working on if it isn't clear.

Your saved context can include your role, current projects, preferred level of detail, and common tasks. Some chatbots also offer account-wide custom instructions or personalization. Use those for broadly applicable preferences, and project instructions for a particular job. Keep confidential work context only in systems approved for it.

Projects can keep instructions and reference material together. Memory is a separate feature whose behavior depends on the product and settings. Don't assume it remembers everything accurately: save important decisions explicitly and supply the current version when it matters. ChatGPT project help and Claude project help explain their controls.

The project-folder guide shows how to gather and save reusable context. Keep lasting preferences in the reusable file; put this trip's dates and bookings in the individual brief. Afterward, add the few lessons that would change your next decision.

docs.title: Teach it your voice
docs.text:
If every draft sounds like it came from a corporate newsletter, give it examples of your own writing. Ask what patterns it sees, then turn those observations into a short style guide. Add a few annotated passages explaining what you like about them.

Test the guide on something you've already written. Keep what helps and correct what doesn't. The voice-file walkthrough includes the full process and a Chatbot setup tab.

docs.title: Check what you're going to rely on
docs.text:
Chatbots can be useful at drafting, explaining, brainstorming, reorganizing information, and comparing supplied material. They can also invent a citation, misread a table, or give confident advice built on a false assumption.

  • Facts and references: open the cited source and check that it supports the claim. A plausible-looking citation is not evidence.
  • Dates, prices, and availability: ask for current sources when search is available, then verify the details that affect your decision.
  • Calculations: ask for a calculator, spreadsheet, or code-based calculation where available. Check important totals and the inputs used.
  • Summaries: spot-check the original, especially names, deadlines, exceptions, and numbers. Asking for a supporting quotation or page reference makes checking easier.
  • Consequential decisions: use the output to prepare questions and organize evidence. Medical, legal, and financial judgments still need the appropriate expertise.

“Don't make things up” is a useful instruction, not a reliability guarantee. Check the reasoning as well as the facts.

For a substantial plan, get a fresh-chat critique. Give the reviewer the goal and constraints as well as the draft. A fresh chat offers another look; it can still share the first model's blind spots.

docs.title: Keep the prompts that worked
docs.text:
When a request produces something useful, save it with a brief note about why it worked. Replace the one-off details with placeholders. Keep a couple of good outputs beside it so you can judge whether the prompt still works after you change it.

Useful candidates include a paper summary for a nontechnical reader, a meeting-notes-to-action-items request, a recommendation-letter outline, or a check for logical gaps in a draft.

Start with a text file or a note. You don't need a prompt-management system. The preferences template and prompt assistant give you a starting point.

If you later use an agent, those saved prompts can become the starting point for a reusable skill.

For other ways to work, see voice dictation, meeting transcription, and working with a collection of documents in NotebookLM. Recording, uploading, or connecting accounts still depends on what's permitted in your setting.

Back to Get ahead of the curve

docs.title: Scout and curate new AI tips
docs.text:
Tips arrive every day — X especially, but also blogs, newsletters, Slack, the occasional email from a friend who just discovered something. It's a firehose. The temptation is to drink from it. The result is churn.

Six questions I keep running into:

  • Which tips are worth adopting?
  • Where do I store them so they're not lost?
  • How do I remember the ones I already filed?
  • How do I prioritize what to actually integrate?
  • How do I get a tip into my workflow, not just a notes file?
  • How do I avoid wrecking a working setup with a bad addition?

This is the system I built for myself. It might work for you. You may want to adapt it. Either way, here it is.

I use three skills to collect ideas, decide which are useful, and put selected improvements to work. Run them when you have something worth investigating; they do not run on a schedule unless you arrange that separately.

  1. Scout — prepare a search from gaps in your existing tips log. Ask it to consult Grok if you want it to run the search too.
  2. Curate — collect tips from saved reports, X bookmarks or email. Compare them with what you already saved, assess their value, and file selected findings in one shared log.
  3. Integrate — turn the useful ideas into concrete changes or investigations. For larger batches, five independent critics help rank them.
  4. Apply — review the proposed changes and have the agent apply the ones you choose. Keep the results for the next round.
graph LR
    S["Scout<br/>prepare · optionally search"]
    C["Curate<br/>reports · bookmarks · email"]
    I["Integrate<br/>rank · propose"]
    A["Apply selected changes<br/>instructions · skills · rules"]
    S --> C --> I --> A
    A -.->|next round| S

/tips-curate offers to invoke /tips-integrate when more than 15 High tips await a decision. You can also run integration on a smaller batch whenever you want.

docs.title: A council, not a checklist
docs.text:
Stage 3 is where this loop differs from a typical "save tips and try them later" practice. One Claude rating its own tips is peer-reviewing your own paper. The model anchors on the framing of the tip and produces convergent praise. I tried that for a few months and ended up with a config full of plausible-sounding additions that didn't compound and weren't worth their maintenance.

The fix is structural disagreement. Five personas in parallel, each told to score from one specific lens and not balance — Maintenance Tax notices that a tip depends on a single-maintainer repo, Catalog Conflict notices it duplicates an existing rule, First-Run notices that the "obvious" first step actually requires three design decisions. The composite scores them; the user approves. The council helps rank the options; you decide which changes to make.

The shared starter kit provides the general Council and review workflows. This tips workflow uses five specialist critics whose instructions are bundled with Tips Integrate. It skips that panel for batches of five or fewer actionable ideas.

docs.title: Meet the five critics
docs.text:
Critic What it asks Catalog Conflict Does this fight something I already do? Maintenance Tax What will this cost me in six months? Compounder Does this make other skills better, or sit alone? First-Run Is the 30-minute first step concrete? Skeptic Real practitioner use, or engagement farming?

Each persona scores every candidate tip 1–5 with a single-sentence rationale and a concrete blocking concern or BLOCKING: none. Five personas × N tips = a stack of structured opinions, not a vote.

An illustrative critic response

TIP: 2026-04-12::Use XML tags around few-shot examples
PERSONA: Maintenance Tax
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: XML tag conventions are documented Anthropic guidance
  and survive model upgrades; no third-party dependency to rot.
BLOCKING: none
How the ranking works

The score is the mean of the returned critic scores, minus 0.1 for each blocker. The agent shows missing perspectives and disagreements alongside the ranking. At least three of the five critics must return; otherwise it stops and retains the batch for a later attempt.

The top seven become concrete proposals, starting with the first three. Remaining candidates stay visible. A score does not authorize an edit: the agent shows the proposed changes and applies those you approve, or those already covered by your request.

docs.title: A tip's journey, end to end
docs.text:
Here is an illustrative tip, walked through the full loop:

1. Discover2. Curate3. Integrate4. Applied

A blog post crosses my feed. I forward it to myself with @toself in the subject — works from my phone, my laptop, anywhere. Gmail tags it automatically.

To: me
Subject: @toself xml tags in skills
Body: https://example.com/post — author shows that
wrapping few-shot examples in <example>...</example>
cuts misparses by ~30%.

When I run it with the email connection configured, /tips-curate reads unread @ToSelf email, classifies each, fetches link content where it can, and rates the result High / Medium / Low. The approved entry lands in the tips log:

## 2026-04-12

### Use XML tags around few-shot examples [skill-design] [prompting] [high]
- **Source:** [author] (Apr 11, 2026)
- **Insight:** Wrap few-shot examples in <example> tags inside
  skill prompts — improves Claude's parsing of multi-example
  sections vs. plain text.
- **Action:** Add an XML-tag convention to CLAUDE.md skill
  authoring rules; retrofit two highest-traffic skills.
- **URL:** https://example.com/post

Two weeks later the high-tip backlog crosses 15. /tips-curate offers to invoke /tips-integrate. Five personas dispatch in parallel against the batch. The composite for this tip:

Catalog Conflict:  4   (no existing rule on tag conventions)
Maintenance Tax:   4   (Anthropic guidance, no rot)
Compounder:        5   (lifts every skill that uses examples)
First-Run:         5   (one CLAUDE.md line; clear retrofit list)
Skeptic:           3   (one author, but evidence is concrete)

composite = 4.2 − 0 = 4.2  →  rank #2  →  first proposals to review

The agent proposes a direct change. I see the diff:

 ## Skill authoring rules

+- Wrap multi-example sections in <example>...</example> tags.
+  Improves Claude's parsing reliability vs. plain prose.
 - Skills under 300 lines unless layered structure required.

I ask it to apply the change. It updates the file, checks the result, and records the completed integration so the same tip is not proposed again.

Investigation tasks (Type B — tips that need design work before any file change) take a different exit: instead of a direct edit, the council writes a one-line entry to your learning catalog's INBOX for triage at your own pace.

docs.title: What it has actually changed
docs.text:
A sample of recent council-approved edits from the log:

Tip Resulting change Wrap few-shot examples in <example> tags New rule line in CLAUDE.md skill-authoring section Use action verbs over "be thorough" in depth-injection Updated prompt-preferences.md depth tier table Pre-flight glob for persona files before council dispatch New rule in agent-dispatch.md Cap context-management thresholds in absolute tokens (4.7 / 1M) Rewrote context-management.md warning thresholds

Most weeks produce one or two direct edits. Most of the council's output is investigation tasks — tips that need a design decision before any file change — which land in the learning catalog INBOX rather than the config.

First runs are mostly investigations, not edits.

The council often defers tips into research tasks rather than rule changes. That's the system working — it's protecting your config from churn. Direct-edit volume rises as your setup grows and the skill has more concrete files to point at.

docs.title: /tips-scout — prepare a useful search
docs.text:
Reads the last 14 days of the shared tips log and any configured active tasks, then prepares a search prompt that emphasizes gaps and questions relevant to your work. It saves that prompt. Invoking the skill alone does not call another AI.

To ask Grok to run it too:

/tips-scout Prepare this week's search and ask Grok to run it. Save the response so I can curate the findings.

That uses the starter kit's /ask-agents connection to the official Grok subscription tool. It is a source-search consultation, not a claim to invoke a separate DeepSearch mode. If the connection is missing, the agent saves the prompt and explains what needs connecting. It does not silently switch providers or ask you to paste into a browser.

Tips Scout folder →

docs.title: /tips-curate — collect, assess and file
docs.text:
Handles bookmarks, email tips and saved research reports in one workflow. The former /tips-bookmarks skill is now part of this one. You can use any of these sources; they do not all need to be connected.

/tips-curate Read the scout report we just saved and suggest what is worth keeping.

Naming a report processes that report alone. A general /tips-curate request checks configured bookmarks and tips email. It compares URLs and underlying claims with the shared log, preserves source links, and proposes High, Medium or Low ratings. It also notes whether an idea applies to Claude, Codex, both, or belongs on a watch list.

After you select what to keep, it saves the entries and verifies them before marking source items processed. Failed or deferred items remain available. /tips-curate dryrun shows proposed results without saving files or changing email/bookmark state.

Tips Curate folder →

docs.title: /tips-integrate — turn ideas into changes
docs.text:
Reads the tips and configured instructions, skills and other targets. For larger batches, five fresh critics rank up to 15 candidates. For five or fewer, it goes straight to proposals. It shows concrete edits for ideas that can be applied now and queues investigations for those that need more work.

/tips-integrate Show me which saved tips would be most useful for my setup and what you would change.

The agent applies selected changes, checks them and records what happened. An investigation queued for later is not counted as an implemented improvement. Deferred and overflow items remain pending rather than disappearing after a run.

Tips Integrate folder →

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Ask your agent to install the whole skill folders, including their supporting references:

Help me set up tips-scout, tips-curate and tips-integrate from the skills folder at github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman. Keep my existing customizations. Use one shared tips log across my AI apps, and walk me through connecting the sources I want to use.

These are public adaptations of my workflow. They include the critic instructions and a starting search prompt, but your accounts, log and target files need configuring. Live connections depend on your app and setup.

The default tips folder is ~/.claude-assistant/tips/; reuse an existing location if you have one. Keep logs and state outside the installed skill folders so an update does not replace them. Start with /tips-curate dryrun, then save a small batch and try /tips-integrate dryrun before applying changes.

docs.title: Optional email collection
docs.text: If you want to forward tips to yourself, connect your email and create a Gmail label called @ToSelf. An optional filter can apply that label to messages whose subject contains @toself. The agent can help set this up. Saved reports work without an email connection; bookmark collection needs a connection that can read your saved posts.

docs.title: When to run
docs.text:
Skill When it is useful /tips-scout You want to look for ideas relevant to your current work. /tips-curate You have new bookmarks, tips email or a research report to sort through. /tips-integrate You are ready to decide which ideas to put into practice.

There is no minimum backlog or fixed schedule. If you use both Claude and Codex, keep one shared log; the route attached to each idea helps the agent choose the right place to apply it.

docs.title: The tips log
docs.text:
The curate step writes approved tips to a dated, tagged markdown file that grows over time. Each entry records what you found, where it came from, and what to do about it. The worked journey above illustrates the format — date, tags like [prompting] or [skill-design], source link, insight, and a concrete next action.

After six months mine had 85+ entries. You don't need to remember what you read last month — search the log by keyword or tag, or point Claude at it and ask "what do I have on agent patterns?" The log becomes institutional memory that survives across sessions.

Browse a snapshot of my actual tips log to see what this looks like at scale.

docs.title: The learning catalog
docs.text:
The tips log captures discoveries. The learning catalog captures decisions — what's worth doing, what you've tried, what you've dismissed.

When /tips-integrate flags a tip as needing research before action (Type B), it lands in the catalog's INBOX section. You review periodically and promote each item to a tier:

Tier Meaning HIGH Clear payoff, do soon MEDIUM Worth evaluating, not urgent LOW Not worth pursuing now; kept for reference DONE Implemented and working REJECTED Assessed and dismissed; won't resurface

Items always enter via INBOX — the skill doesn't make priority calls on your behalf.

Each HIGH and MEDIUM entry carries plain-English context: what it is, why it matters for you, and next step. The format is designed for future-you who's forgotten the original tip. A DONE entry looks like:

Item Was Completed arjunkmrm/recall Cross-session search — /recall searches 1,918 past conversations by keyword Mar 3, 2026

DONE and REJECTED entries are never deleted — they prevent you from re-evaluating the same thing six months later.

docs.title: Browse real examples
docs.text:
The kinds of workflows and resources the pipeline is designed to capture and evaluate. Worth browsing to see what's out there:

  • Boris Tane: How I Use Claude Code — The research-annotate-implement workflow. One of the highest-rated tips in my log.
  • Anthropic's Official Skills Library — Anthropic's own example skills, including a document plugin for PDFs and spreadsheets.
  • Awesome Claude Skills — Community-curated list of skills, patterns, and tools. Good scouting territory.
  • Anthropic Skills Cookbooks — Tutorial notebooks for building custom skills from scratch.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
/tips-curate: Tips log location, Gmail label name, batch size, quality thresholds — all configurable by editing the skill file directly.

/tips-integrate: Source selection, target files, and investigation destination. Keep state and pending decisions when changing the configuration.

The other input channel: your own corrections

You can also improve your setup from what happens during work. The continuous improvement guide explains how to capture corrections and use them to revise your writing guidance.

docs.title: The Cost Reality
docs.text:
No Claude Code required

What building an AI workflow costs, who it makes sense for, and who should start smaller.

docs.title: The Full Stack
docs.text:
Prices as of February 2026 — AI tool pricing changes frequently. Verify at each tool's website for current rates.

Here's what my current setup costs per month:

Tool What It Does Monthly Cost Claude Max (Opus 4.6 + Sonnet 4.6) Primary AI tool + Claude Code ~$100 ChatGPT Plus Deep Research, web search, images ~$20 Wispr Flow Dictation (Mac + iPhone) ~$10 Granola Meeting transcription $0–14 Total ~$140/month

That's ~$1,700/year. It's real money.

docs.title: Professors and Senior Researchers
docs.text:
If you have a research budget, this is easy to justify. At a $20/hour RA rate, this costs the equivalent of about 7 RA hours per month. If it saves you more than 7 hours — and it will, once configured — the math works.

Many universities allow software subscriptions on research accounts. Check with your grants manager.

docs.title: Organizations and NGOs
docs.text: For professionals managing projects, teams, and communications, the productivity gains from email triage, meeting management, and document drafting justify the cost quickly. Especially for people whose time is expensive relative to the subscription.

docs.title: Who Should Start Smaller
docs.text:
Graduate students and early-career researchers without institutional support face a real trade-off. $1,700/year is not trivial on a graduate stipend.

The minimum viable setup:

Tool Cost What You Get Claude Pro ~$20/mo Full chatbot + basic Claude Code access Apple/Google Dictation Free Built-in dictation (less polished than Wispr) Zoom transcription Free with Zoom Basic meeting transcripts Total ~$20/month

You lose the power tools, but you still get the core: a strong AI chatbot with structured prompting, basic dictation, and basic transcription. You can always upgrade as your budget and needs grow.

docs.title: ROI Framework
docs.text:
Conservative estimate: If this system saves you 5 hours per month of administrative work, and your time is worth $40/hour (a modest estimate for a professional), that's $200/month in recovered time. Net gain: $60/month.

Realistic estimate with a configured system: Once you have skills running for email triage, meeting processing, and project management, 10-15 hours/month of savings is achievable. At $40/hour, that's $400-600/month in recovered time.

The honest caveat: There's an upfront time investment to learn the tools and build the system. I spent many hours over several weeks getting my setup where it is now. The ROI is real but not instant.

Data policies differ by product

Claude Code uses the Anthropic API — your conversations are not used for model training under the current API data policy. Claude.ai (the browser version) is a consumer product with a different policy — check your account settings for data usage preferences. If you work with sensitive research data, this distinction matters. See Privacy for more.

docs.title: What to Try First
docs.text:
If you're not sure whether this is worth it, here's a low-risk sequence:

  1. Week 1: Sign up for Claude Pro ($20/mo) and work through your first session. Then use it for one real work task daily.
  2. Week 2: Try Wispr Flow (free trial available). See if dictation changes how you interact with AI.
  3. Week 3: If you're getting value, try Granola for your next few meetings.
  4. Week 4: If you want to go deeper, install Claude Code (Install Guide) and try the Toolkit path.

At each step, you can stop. You don't need the full stack to get value. The chatbot alone, used well, is worth the subscription for most knowledge workers.

docs.title: Other council and adversarial review skills
docs.text:
You do not need my starter kit to try this way of working. This is an occasionally updated list of other implementations worth exploring. Their authors make different choices about council members, synthesis, and repeated review.

Last checked: October 22, 2026. Descriptions below come from the projects’ own documentation. These are options to investigate, not tools I have tested or ranked.

docs.title: Reasoning, decisions, and research
docs.text: Skill What its authors describe What to know before choosing it Quorum — GTuritto Challenges plans, compares approaches, and reviews work in Codex, Claude Code, and other compatible tools. Its Full mode uses independent workers when the tool supports them. Mini mode uses several perspectives in one conversation; it is not the independent council described in this guide. The Council — DantesPeak85 Claude asks Codex and Gemini for independent analyses, then combines their recommendations. Intended for Claude Code with the external tools connected. Read its current setup requirements and version notes. Adversarial Research Loop — CodeReclaimers An outside model challenges a research project; Claude investigates the concerns with tests and evidence across repeated rounds. Closest to the research-and-revision part of the workflow. It assumes a project whose claims can be investigated, rather than only editing a piece of prose.

docs.title: Primarily for code and technical plans
docs.text:
Skill What its authors describe What to know before choosing it Review Council — ianpcook Several review perspectives examine the same code change, then an independent critic challenges the proposed findings. Packaged for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and compatible tools. Its output is a code-review verdict, so it is not a direct replacement for a general proposal-writing council. Adversarial Review — j-wang Fresh Claude and Codex reviews, with optional additional models, followed by verification of the findings against the code. Runs from Claude Code and needs the chosen external tools. The design emphasizes checking whether objections are supported. Review Council — DeployHQ Independent model reviews of code or plans, a challenge to their findings, and a final judge that prioritizes the result. A more elaborate Claude Code plugin. Read its model and tool requirements before choosing it for a small task.

Follow the installation guide in the linked repository; the packages and command names differ. Ask your agent whether the chosen skill runs separate subagents, which models it can call, and where it saves the result. Then return to step two of Council basics to choose your members.

docs.title: Dial-Back Discipline
docs.text:
I spent a week in April stripping the word CRITICAL out of my skill files. Also YOU MUST, ABSOLUTELY, IMPORTANT, and most ALL-CAPS emphasis. Nineteen dial-backs across six skill files. The skills got shorter and they started producing better output.

Here's why, and how to do the same audit on your own skills.

docs.title: Why ceremonial emphasis backfires
docs.text:
Early in the Claude Code era, prompts that told the model YOU MUST DO X or CRITICAL: NEVER Y seemed to work. The model took them seriously. So skill libraries filled up with capitalized directives, warnings, and emphatic hedges.

Something changed in Claude 4.5 and persists in 4.7. Anthropic's own prompting guide calls out the issue directly: anti-laziness language like "be thorough," "think carefully," or CRITICAL/MUST over-triggers the model, especially in tool-use contexts. The model spends extra tokens deliberating about whether it's being thorough enough, runs extra verification passes, and drifts away from the actual task. The emphasis that used to ensure compliance now costs performance.

You can test this yourself. Take a skill with a pile of CRITICAL: YOU MUST ABSOLUTELY... prefixes and run it against a simple task. Strip the emphasis and run the same task. The stripped version is usually faster and at least as accurate.

docs.title: The two categories of emphasis
docs.text:
Not all emphasis is wrong. A useful audit distinguishes two kinds:

Ceremonial emphasis — used to signal seriousness to the reader (me, writing the skill) rather than to constrain the model. Most of the CRITICAL labels I'd written over time fell here. I was using them as section markers, or to reassure myself that the skill handled an edge case, or to make a point stand out when I re-read the file. The model doesn't benefit from these.

Load-bearing emphasis — used because the consequence of skipping the rule is genuine user harm: an email sent without approval, a file deleted, a filter created that runs forever. Here the emphasis is earning its keep. A CRITICAL label on "never send an email without explicit user confirmation" is worth keeping because the failure mode is real and irreversible.

The audit rule: if you can remove the emphasis and the worst-case outcome is just a slightly worse skill output, it's ceremonial. If removing it risks a user consequence that can't be undone, it's load-bearing.

docs.title: What to strip, by example
docs.text:
Before:

CRITICAL: YOU MUST follow this sequence exactly.

  1. Read the config file
  2. Extract team members
  3. Filter by active status

IMPORTANT: Never skip step 3 or you will get stale data.

After:

Follow this sequence:

  1. Read the config file
  2. Extract team members
  3. Filter by active status — skipping this leaves stale members in the output.

Two things changed. The CRITICAL/IMPORTANT wrapper is gone. The warning about step 3 is now in-line with the step itself, framed as a positive consequence ("skipping this leaves stale members") rather than a negative injunction ("Never skip").

Another before:

YOU MUST NOT use markdown headers in the output.

After:

Output format: plain paragraphs, no headers.

The constraint is the same; the wording is calmer. Positive description of what to do beats a capitalized ban on what not to.

docs.title: What to keep
docs.text:
Kept as load-bearing in my own skills after the audit:

  • "CRITICAL: never send an email without explicit user approval" — sending is irreversible, the failure mode is real.
  • "YOU MUST NOT create Gmail filters without confirmation" — filters run 24/7 without Claude, mis-created filters are a long-lived problem.
  • "CRITICAL: do not modify the live production database" — destructive, irreversible.

Everything else got dialed back. The skill files are about 15% shorter. Behavior is the same or slightly better.

docs.title: How to run the audit
docs.text:
About 45 minutes per skill if you already know it well. For a library of six to ten heavy skills, plan a half-day.

  1. Grep for the flagged words: 
    grep -nE "CRITICAL|YOU MUST|ABSOLUTELY|IMPORTANT:|NEVER " ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md
  2. For each hit, ask the two-category question: Ceremonial or load-bearing? If the worst case of removing it is "slightly worse output," it's ceremonial. Strip it.
  3. Rewrite as positive description where possible. "Do X; skipping X means Y" beats "NEVER skip X or ABSOLUTELY Y."
  4. Keep real safety gates. Don't cut the approval requirements on irreversible operations. Re-read the rewrite and check that the load-bearing cases still read as blocking.
  5. Run the skill against a familiar task. Compare length of output, quality of output, and tool-call count against the pre-audit baseline. In my audit, every skill got slightly faster; none got worse.
  6. Record the dial-backs. Keep a one-line log of what was cut from which skill. Useful if a regression shows up later — you know what to try putting back first.

docs.title: Related patterns
docs.text:
Positive examples beat negative rules. "Write in flowing prose with no headers or bullets" beats "don't use markdown." When you have to forbid something, pair the ban with a concrete positive.

Action verbs, not vague adjectives. "Be thorough" is empty. "Compare your approach against [named standard]" is specific. Depth comes from action verbs, not emphasis.

Bookend pattern, not repetition. If a constraint really matters for a long prompt, state it at the top and restate it at the end. That's more effective than capitalizing it in the middle.

docs.title: What this costs you
docs.text:
One real tradeoff: dial-back discipline makes your skill files less legible to you, the author, when you re-open them months later. The capitalized warnings used to serve as visual bookmarks. Stripping them means you can't scan the file as quickly for "where was that important bit?"

Two fixes: use markdown section headers (##, ###) as structural navigation. And add a brief one-sentence summary at the top of each skill that names the things that would be most dangerous to change. That gives future-you the visual anchor without feeding the ceremony back to the model.
